title: Why AI is an even bigger deal than you think
chineseTitle: 为什么 AI 的颠覆性远超你的想象：Netflix 联合创始人与可汗学院 CEO 的深度对话
speaker: Reed Hastings & Sal Khan
speakerTitle: Netflix 联合创始人 & 可汗学院 CEO
quote: The biggest uncertainty for everybody is how fast is AI getting better and how fast will it be getting better going forward.
quoteTranslation: 摆在所有人面前最大的未知数在于：AI 的进化到底有多快？未来又将以何种加速度重塑一切？

segments.title: 开场对谈：25年、10亿美元教育慈善的反思
segments.original: So Reed, education, which a lot of people -- I don't know how many know how active you are in education, education philanthropy, charter schools, etc. What are you doing in that space? On the Board of Khan Academy and generally I've been working for the last 25 years to try to find ways to make in particular U.S. schools, but some international, work better and have better outcomes for kids. And I would say after a billion dollars in 25 years, we're down below where I started. So it's a hard problem. And what do you -- you know, we heard about the risks of ed tech, but you are investing in ed tech, you're giving to ed tech. What are your thoughts? What's the trade-off there? Why do you continue to potentially believe there?
segments.translation:
Sal：Reed，关于教育领域——不知道有多少人了解你在教育、教育慈善和特许学校等方面有多么活跃。你在那个领域具体在做什么？
Reed：我在可汗学院的董事会，过去 25 年里我一直在努力探索如何让特别是美国的学校（包括一些国际学校）运转得更好，让孩子们取得更好的成果。但我必须说，在投入了 25 年和 10 亿美元之后，我们的现状甚至比我刚开始时还要低。所以这是个极其棘手的难题。
Sal：那么你怎么看——我们经常听到关于教育科技（EdTech）风险的讨论，但你一直在投资教育科技，一直在捐助教育科技。你的真实想法是什么？这其中的权衡是什么？为什么你依然坚信这个方向？

segments.title: 蒸汽机与电动机隐喻：传统课堂的根本摩擦力
segments.original: You know, in the 18th century most factories were steam engine driven. They have a big steam engine rotating rods and pulleys and belts and drove the factory very efficient. And then electricity came in and they replaced the steam engine with an electric engine thinking that it was going to help a lot, and productivity didn't increase at all, and they were puzzled. And then they realized the limiting factor is the power distribution system, all these spinning rods and mechanical power. And they ripped that out and just put in small electric motors for each device, then they could move things around, fit them in better because it wasn't aligned to the spinning. They could have variable speed, turn different motors on and off, and then productivity increased dramatically. So it's a classic kind of economic surprise lesson. And it's always stuck with me because I think that's what we're seeing, which is we keep doing things to improve classroom education, but the fundamental power distribution is 25 kids stuck at the same level.
segments.translation: 你看，在 18 世纪，大多数工厂都是由蒸汽机驱动的。工厂里有一台巨大的蒸汽机，通过旋转的传动轴、滑轮和皮带带动整座工厂运转，在当时非常高效。后来电力出现了，他们把蒸汽机换成了一台大型电动机，以为这样能大幅提升效率，结果生产率根本没有增长，大家都百思不得其解。后来他们终于意识到，真正的瓶颈在于‘动力分配系统’——那些沉重的旋转连杆和机械传动。于是他们彻底拆除了那套系统，为每一台设备单独安装了小型电动机。这样他们就可以自由重排设备、灵活布局，不再受限于传动轴的位置。不同电机可以实现变速、随时启停，工厂的生产率这才迎来了爆发式增长。这是一个经典的经济学启示，我一直铭记于心，因为这正是我们在教育中看到的现象：我们不断尝试各种方法来改进课堂，但底层的‘动力分配’机制仍然是 25 个孩子被困在同一个步调上。

segments.title: 一对一导师与 Bloom 效应：个性化学习的突破口
segments.original: And the theory is if each of us had an individual human tutor -- so imagine you go to school, you have your normal social activities, when it comes to learning, you get an individual who's going to sit down with you, and then they can do Khan Academy or they can do color book or whatever is appropriate, that learning would be massively increased. And there was a famous study 40 years ago, Bloom, that documented this. And now a friend of mine, Ben Summers, is redoing that study but at much bigger scale. And I think what we're going to see is the key to much more learning -- where middle school kids know all of the high school curriculum, high school knows all of the college, much better outcomes -- will be individualized education. How do you score that with what Jonathan Haidt said? Look, these screens, I mean at least it's a correlation, we don't know causal yet, but it seems to be distracting, it seems to correlate with some test scores going down. Is it an all-or-nothing type of thing? I'm a huge fan of Jonathan, totally agree with all his zip-up phones and don't use phones. And I think you guys clarified he likes offline tablets, that's fine. It's the internet that's the problem, not the physical device. So the individualized tutoring we're doing is with humans, they can use some technology if they want. But then obviously that's cost prohibitive because it's about $100,000 per kid per year.
segments.translation:
这个理论的核心是：如果我们每个人都能拥有一位专属的人类导师——想象一下你去上学，有正常的社交活动，而一旦进入学习环节，就有一位专属老师坐在你身边，带着你做可汗学院、或者涂色书、或者任何适合你的内容，学习效果就会产生质的飞跃。40 年前著名的布鲁姆（Bloom）研究就证实了这一点。现在我的朋友 Ben Summers 正在更大规模上重做这项研究。我认为我们即将见证：让初中生掌握高中全部课程、让高中生通晓大学知识的终极钥匙，就是‘个性化教育’。
Sal：那你怎么看 Jonathan Haidt 的观点？他说屏幕至少存在相关性，虽然因果关系尚未定论，但屏幕似乎会分散注意力并导致考试成绩下滑。这对你来说是非黑即白的吗？
Reed：我是 Jonathan 的超级粉丝，完全赞同他把手机封存起来、在学校禁用的主张。大家也澄清过，他支持离线平板，这没问题——问题出在互联网的无休止干扰，而不是电子设备本身。我们现在做的个性化辅导是靠真人导师，但显而易见，其成本高到令人望而却步——每个孩子每年要花费大约 10 万美元。

segments.title: AI 导师超越人类：学校三大职能的重新分工
segments.original: So then the hard challenge becomes how do we use AI to approximate that human and provide everyone an individualized education as AI gets better. Current AI is not good enough to do that, but in three years we've gone from ChatGPT-3.5 and barely being able to do high school math to just incredible intelligence. And that's likely to just continue to double, double, double and get better and better and better. So there is a world where the AI I think will be able to match and beat the human individual tutor. And what does that world look like? Let's just say it's in 10 years. Are you imagining that you're just socializing and then you go to this AI tutor, but are you imagining there's no human teacher? What do you think happens to that role, that profession? Well, let's think about schools. So three big purposes: One is create good citizens. Another is give economic opportunity to the kids. And then the other is socialization, social emotional learning, how to work with other people, adults outside of your family. Only in the first part is really where online is really good. And what we want to do is have teachers be able to focus on social emotional learning. They become really helping maturity, interpersonal skills, values clarification, all those higher-level things.
segments.translation:
因此，真正的艰巨挑战就变成了：随着 AI 越来越强，我们如何利用 AI 来逼近真人导师的能力，为每个人提供专属的个性化教育？当前的 AI 还不足以完全做到这一点，但在短短三年内，我们见证了从 ChatGPT-3.5 勉强做高中数学题，演进到现在令人惊叹的高超智能。而且这种能力很可能会继续以翻倍、再翻倍的节奏不断进化。所以在未来的世界里，我认为 AI 完全有能力匹敌甚至超越人类一对一导师。
Sal：那会是一个怎样的世界？假设是在 10 年后，难道学校里就没有人类教师了吗？这个职业会发生什么变化？
Reed：让我们思考一下学校的三大核心职能：第一是培养合格公民；第二是为孩子们提供经济与发展机会；第三是社交与社会情感学习（SEL），学会如何与家人以外的人和成年人协作相处。线上或技术真正擅长的主要是知识与技能传授。而我们希望的是让教师能够把全部精力解放出来，专注于社会情感学习——帮助孩子走向成熟、培养人际交往能力、树立价值观等更高层面的素养。

segments.title: 告别‘讲台圣人’：教师角色向高阶引导者的跃迁
segments.original: And I just want to double-click on that. You still see a major role for the human teacher and the human classroom. You just see that role shifting. So most teachers today, their pride center is teaching and connecting and understanding the material. Some part of that is really connecting on a personal level with the student. That part is the social emotional. But in terms of transferring information, what educators cynically call 'sage on a stage', it's eliminating 'sage on a stage' as a teaching modality. And so it's really just focused on the individual. What would education be if there was no mass teaching? And to be fair, if you went to an ed school 20 years ago, this is what they were preaching: differentiated instruction, active learning, don't be 'sage on the stage', have a Socratic discussion, do a simulation. So the teacher moves up the value chain and is able to facilitate and drive a lot of that active learning, which is better for everyone. I think it's more fun for the teacher. And the other part is once you can do a lot of this in software, you can do it globally. It's really hard to scale up the teacher force, but software is pretty inexpensive to make globally available.
segments.translation:
Sal：我想深入探讨一下这一点。你依然认为人类教师和真实的线下课堂扮演着核心角色，只是这个角色正在发生转型。
Reed：没错。今天大多数老师的成就感来源在于传授知识和讲解材料，其中一部分是与学生建立真挚的情感连接——这就是社会情感层面。但是在信息灌输方面，正如教育界常讽刺的‘讲台上的圣人’（sage on a stage），AI 将彻底终结这种填鸭式的大班讲授模式。教育将真正回归个体。如果不再有‘一刀切’的集体灌输，教育会变成什么样？其实 20 年前教育学院就在提倡这些：分层教学、主动学习、不要当讲台圣人、开展苏格拉底式讨论与实战模拟。因此，教师实际上是走向了价值链的高端，去引导和激发深度的主动学习，这对所有人都是更好的体验，教师也会觉得教学更有乐趣。另一方面，一旦将这些能力固化在软件中，就能实现全球化普及——培养数百万优秀教师极难规模化，但软件却能以极低成本惠及全世界每一个角落。

segments.title: 加盟 Anthropic 董事会：穿越 AI 传送门与安全使命
segments.original: Getting gears a little bit, because your other board you're on isn't obviously very related to this: Anthropic. Actually I'm just curious, what made you join that board? What's it like at those board meetings when I'm assuming y'all talk about pressures from the White House, how your new model might break all software? Tell us what you can. Yeah, it's a lot like your board meeting, talking about the software and what it can do and how it needs to get better. So the mission of the company is very clear: it's not maximizing profits. It's that we're successful -- humanity. How do we get into the age of AI successfully crossing through sort of this portal? And they recognize it's going to be very challenging, and they're very dedicated to having that happen. Enrolling out AI and having the incredible beneficial outcomes -- whether that's self-driving, whether that's gene editing, whether that's curing cancer. 10, 20 years from now, it's very likely we'll have pretty abundant energy, we will have amazing health outcomes, so much positive outcome from the AI infusion into science. And I would say Anthropic is serious about helping us manage or avoid most of the downside.
segments.translation:
Sal：换个话题，你加入的另一个董事会似乎和教育没有直接关系：Anthropic。我很好奇，是什么契机让你加入了他们的董事会？在那些董事会上是怎样的场景？我猜你们会讨论来自白宫的监管压力，或者你们的新模型会不会颠覆所有软件？能和我们分享一下吗？
Reed：哈哈，其实和可汗学院的董事会挺像的，都是讨论软件的能力以及如何把它做得更好。Anthropic 这家公司的使命非常明确：它的首要目标不是追求利润最大化，而是为了全人类的成功。我们如何才能平稳穿过 AI 时代的这扇传送门？他们深知这充满挑战，并且全力以赴确保安全平稳过渡。在释放 AI 潜力的同时带来巨大的福祉——无论是完全自动驾驶、基因编辑还是治愈癌症。在未来 10 到 20 年内，我们极有可能迎来充裕的清洁能源和颠覆性的医疗突破。AI 融入科学将带来无数积极成果，而 Anthropic 正在极其严肃地致力于帮助人类规避和管理绝大多数潜在负面风险。

segments.title: 大模型竞逐与超级组织演进：比互联网更大的浪潮
segments.original: And at the same time, moving very fast, the hyperspeed. It feels like almost every few weeks there's something new, and it's very tangible in what it might do for work. How are y'all balancing that in Anthropic instead of just saying go, go, go? You know, I think all of the big models are improving rapidly, and you're probably going to see them go certain months on the lead in certain areas over time. And frankly, it's good for the country if we have three really successful models to choose from. When I visited there, I tangibly felt that they were pioneering completely new ways of running an organization, new ways of developing product. I think it was something like 'cowork' was, what was it, a week or two that it was essentially built primarily by the AI itself? What will an organization look like in the future? Yeah, I don't know that most companies will come to look like Anthropic. If you happen to be a pure software company, then it might be relevant. But broadly across the economy, I think everyone is figuring out -- it's a bigger version of the internet wave, where all companies around the world, organizations, governments, militaries are scrambling to figure out how to use AI well.
segments.translation:
Sal：但与此同时，技术迭代的速度是超光速的。几乎每隔几周就有全新突破，而且能切实改变工作方式。Anthropic 是如何在狂飙突进与审慎克制之间保持平衡的？
Reed：我认为所有头部大模型都在迅猛演进，随着时间推移，不同模型会在特定领域轮流领跑几个月。坦白讲，如果整个国家能有三款极其顶尖的模型可供选择，这是一件大好事。
Sal：我去 Anthropic 参观时，真切地感受到他们正在开创一种全新的组织运作方式和产品研发模式。比如像某些协作功能，据说一两周内主要全靠 AI 自身编写完成。未来的企业组织会变成什么样？
Reed：我不认为大多数传统公司都会变得像 Anthropic 一样。如果你是一家纯软件公司，那可能会很像。但放眼整个宏观经济，我认为大家正在经历一场比互联网更大的技术浪潮——全球所有的企业、机构、政府和军队都在争先恐后地探索如何善用 AI。

segments.title: 技术扩散周期与反常现象：放射科医生的逆向启示
segments.original: Related to that, people are talking about it with software engineering, call centers. A startup has a call center in the Philippines, they're going to lay off 80%, that's 7% of that country's GDP. How are you thinking about jobs? Look, if you look over the last 200 years, there have been a bunch of dislocations, but they happened slowly and over one part of the economy. The danger is, are there multiple that happen in multiple fields? If these happen slowly, people are able to find other roles. So it depends on how fast this all comes. The biggest uncertainty for everybody is how fast is the AI getting better, and how fast will it be getting better going forward? Let's look at self-driving cars. 20 years ago we thought it was going to be pretty fast. It's 20 years later from the 2007 DARPA Grand Challenge, and we're like 0.1% of all miles, maybe 0.01%. So these things take a long time to actually mature and diffuse. Another example: Geoffrey Hinton won the Nobel Prize for his work on neural nets, the father of AI. In 2016, he said: 'Stop training radiologists now, because in 5 years, 2021, there would be no need for them.' What's happened instead is as radiology got AI-boosted, the cost came down, you can get an MRI for $300 now. So docs started ordering them more, insurance covered them more, the number of scans went way up. And guess what? We have a shortage in radiologists! Wages climbed to close to $500,000 a year! So even the best intention people in the field can prophecy disaster in radiology and have it be not accurate.
segments.translation:
Sal：关于就业，大家都在讨论软件工程和客服外包中心。我有个朋友的初创公司在菲律宾有客服中心，他们准备裁员 80%，而客服外包占了该国 GDP 的 7%。你是如何思考未来就业冲击的？
Reed：回顾过去 200 年的历史，出现过多次技术替代与结构性失业，但它们通常发生得较为缓慢，且局限在经济的某一个局部领域。如今最大的担忧在于：多领域同时爆发的大规模替代会不会同时发生？如果演进足够缓慢，人们就有时间转行并找到新的角色。所以一切取决于这波浪潮到底有多快。最大的未知数就是 AI 进化的速度到底有多快。以自动驾驶为例，20 年前我们以为它会迅速普及，但距离 2007 年 DARPA 挑战赛已经过去了近 20 年，自动驾驶里程在全社会总里程中占比依然只有 0.1% 甚至 0.01%。技术的成熟与全面扩散需要漫长的时间。另一个经典案例是‘AI 之父’杰弗里·辛顿（Geoffrey Hinton）。2016 年他曾断言：‘立刻停止培养放射科医生，因为 5 年后（2021年）他们将被彻底淘汰。’ 然而实际发生了什么？随着 AI 辅助放射学，核磁共振（MRI）的检查成本大幅降低（美国只要 300 美元），医生开出的检查单激增，医保报销范围扩大，检查总量爆发式增长。结果呢？放射科医生严重短缺，年薪甚至飙升至近 50 万美元！所以即使是业内最顶尖、最权威的专家，对技术淘汰的灾难性预言也可能完全偏离事实。

segments.title: 奇点社会新形态：超高增长、失业与全民主权基金
segments.original: And that makes sense, although something does feel different about this time. And all the people leading these AI labs are talking about not 20 years. They're talking about next year, two years. You're going to have a data center of super intelligent geniuses that can do our work. Do you think they're wrong, or do you think it's a probability? Even if it's a 10% chance that they're right, are you worried that this can lead to political polarization, what happened in globalization can now happen -- what happened in 30 years could happen in two or three? Is that not a concern, or should we start doing something about that? If AI really gets incredible in a very short amount of time, like starts writing itself and self-improving, all of that... When it's invented a new type of learning, when it invents something completely new, then you can say that. But so there are cases where it's pretty fast, and so I think it's important to say we should be ready. Now here's the thing: we talk a bunch about unemployment, what it will do. Every other time we've had big unemployment, it's been a recession, and so the stock market's down and government tax revenues are down. This time, if AI is successful in the way we think it will, I think we're going to see high productivity, high GDP growth, high stock market, and high unemployment. So we'll have money to do things. Think of it like the Alaska Fund, which is oil, or the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund. We need some ideas like that. What are we going to do with all these huge tax revenues that are going to be able to come in with big growth? If we've got a fund which is for the benefit of all citizens, then we may in fact be able to have a path to a glorious and harmonious society. I don't mean UBI -- that's got a bad take to it -- but it's a partial sharing of the rewards, which is again what happened with the Alaska Fund and the Norwegian Fund. That makes sense. Well Reed Hastings, thank you so much, and thanks everyone.
segments.translation:
Sal：这很有道理。但这一次确实让人感觉有所不同——各大 AI 实验室的领跑者谈论的不是 20 年后，而是明年、后年。他们说不久后一个数据中心就能容纳成千上万个超级智能天才来替人类工作。你觉得他们错了吗？哪怕只有 10% 的可能性他们是对的，你是否担心这会引发严重的政治撕裂？过去 30 年全球化带来的冲击，如今可能在两三年内集中爆发。这难道不值得担忧吗？我们是否应该采取行动？
Reed：如果 AI 在极短时间内实现自我编写与自我进化，当它真正发明出一种全新的自主学习范式时，你才能那么断言。但有些突破确实来得非常迅猛，所以我们必须做好万全准备。关于失业问题，有一点与以往截然不同：在历史上，每一次大规模失业都伴随着经济衰退——股市暴跌、政府税收锐减。但这一次，如果 AI 取得了预期的巨大成功，我们将看到一种前所未有的局面：超高生产率、超高 GDP 增长、超高股市估值，与高失业率并存！这意味着全社会将拥有充裕的财富来解决问题。想象一下阿拉斯加永久基金（源自石油收益）或挪威主权财富基金。在高增长带来的海量税收面前，如果我们建立一个惠及全体国民的主权财富基金，让所有人共同分享技术革命的红利，我们完全有可能走向一个繁荣而和谐的社会。我指的不是传统的 UBI（全民无条件基本收入），而是类似主权基金的红利共享机制。
Sal：非常有启发。Reed Hastings，非常感谢你的精彩分享，也谢谢大家！

spoken.meaning: 面临 / 遭遇（极其棘手的瓶颈或强大挑战）

spoken.quote: And after all that, he thinks we're still up against the same fundamental problems in education.

title: How doodling unlocks your imagination
chineseTitle: 涂鸦如何解锁你的想象力：16岁“涂鸦少年”谈AI时代的创作本能
speaker: Joe Whale
speakerTitle: “涂鸦男孩 (The Doodle Boy)” · 英国青年艺术家
quote: Imagination is like a muscle: the more you use it, the stronger it becomes.
quoteTranslation: 想象力宛如肌肉：越锻炼越强健；若弃之不用，便只能仰赖外物。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：I was younger, I used to get told off...
segments.original: I was younger, I used to get told off in class for doodling. I couldn't stop. My teacher would always stop me from doing this. And it was really worrying because as a creative person, it's something that I do naturally. After a few weeks at my art class, I was booked in because I was having this trouble at school. My teacher suggested something unusual. There was a big empty wall in a local restaurant. She asked them if I could draw on it. They said yes. So I started filling the restaurant wall with my artwork. People would come in and watch me while they were eating. Photos started appearing online. Then the local newspaper wrote about it. And suddenly, people all around the world were talking about this kid who couldn't stop doodling.

And it was really worrying because as a creative person, it's something that I do naturally. After a few weeks at my art class, I was booked in because I was having this trouble at school. My teacher suggested something unusual. There was a big empty wall in a local restaurant. She asked them if I could draw on it. They said yes. So I started filling the restaurant wall with my artwork. People would come in and watch me while they were eating. Photos started appearing online. Then the local newspaper wrote about it. And suddenly, people all around the world were talking about this kid who couldn't stop doodling.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：That moment changed my life
segments.original: That moment changed my life. I wasn't even trying to be an artist, but the important thing is how it started. It started with my imagination and parents who didn't disregard but embraced my passion. It started with the freedom to just draw. And that's what I want to talk about today. Because the world is very different than when it was when I was first doodling 10 years ago. Today, it's possible to type prompts into AI, make anything and feel creative. But I believe there will always be value in letting our imaginations be the true driver of our creations. Because imagination is like a muscle. The more you use it, the stronger it becomes. But if you don't use it, it gets weaker. And your body will rely on something else to do it for you.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：Creativity is not encouraged today
segments.original: Creativity is not encouraged today. It's not given value. So it's easy to turn to the tools right in front of us and get an instant result. But you don't learn by going straight to the end. You learn from the journey. Everything begins with a thought, an idea, a meaning, or a vision. That's your imagination, the beginning. And that beginning influences what you do from that point. It's freedom. Imagination is the first step. And direction flows through the creation. You're letting yourself literally wander wherever you wish, the freedom to go anywhere. Because that first step is coming from you and not something else. What I can see is we'll be reliant to replace something we all need and all have. We'll be handing it off just because it's easier.

segments.original: We're rational animals, we have extraordinarily great capabilities in us, but the only way that we realize them, unlike most animals, which kind of mature and develop their powers no matter what, a squirrel becomes a good squirrel with that very little effort. Humans require a great deal of effort to become good versions of what we're supposed to be, and it requires a lot of attention, not just to ourselves, but attention on the part of our parents and teachers, and I think when we fail to flourish, it's not typically because we've had some malicious plan that screwed up our lives, but really we just never had the opportunity to focus on the good plan, so I would think distraction. How about you? That's a great response. We are really high intensity creatures, and we need a lot of attention, we need a lot of explicit care and development to become maybe the best version of ourselves. For me, it's interesting. I think of this sometimes in the context of why do we spend so much money on space exploration? If some of the barriers to human thriving are things like poverty, war, climate change, there's a lot of things at a societal scale that might be keeping us from thriving in the way that we really could, and then there raises the question, why would we spend money on space at all in that context? I think one of the things we could do to help human thriving is we can use space for the benefit of life on Earth, so before we go be a sci-fi space-faring species, maybe we earn our right to go do that someday by showing that we can take really good care of our own planet first, so try to do things in space that would help with human thriving, and my latest favorite one is biology.

segments.title: 第 7 幕：Turns out biology is really different...
segments.original: Turns out biology is really different when you're floating in orbit than when you're on the ground, and so we might be able to do things like cancer cures, Alzheimer's, organoids, testing, all kinds of interesting things that would maybe help humans thrive in a more concrete immediate way on Earth, but leveraging space technology. It strikes me as somebody who's a huge space fan girl, is what I would say, is that having these really concrete and ambitious goals like going to the moon or putting people on the space station sometimes forces us to focus our attention on solving problems that then help us solve problems back here on Earth, and having a big vision like that, sometimes exactly the kick and the pants you need to feel motivated to take on something that in your ordinary life might not feel like it deserves your attention. This is exactly what we want to do in space. How do we build systems that influence the good in each other? Systems that influence the good in each other also have to assume good intentions at the base, and so being able to think about what is the architecture of policy that comes out of the US government, or ways that we could unify people to get them there, and I've recently become really passionate about something completely outside of my domain, so maybe I'm a little over my skis, which is an idea of a national service, not necessarily a military draft.

segments.original: My parents are both ex-military and very supportive of a military, but something that would be like every young person does something for a year when they're 18, and it really unites red and blue state kids and urban and rural kids, and it could be Teach for America, it could be something that's service oriented, also maybe military service oriented, but something like that I think once you get to know the people of your community and your village and your society and your civilization a little bit better, I think you can do a better job of finding the good in them, and then maybe building good systems around them. I love that. I think on my end, there are a few institutions that really roll up their sleeves and do this work of forming people's characters. One is education. Another would be like church and religious organizations, and a third is the media, and everybody likes to talk about how awful whatever fill in the blank social media is, but genuinely print media, the news and various sources still very much forms people's outlook and what they hope for and what they view as their sort of purpose in life. I think we have sorely neglected those institutions, and a lot of people are really on the brink of nihilism I think right now about whether we could still imagine amazing schools, whether we could still imagine on the weekends you going and being with other humans and doing some kind of collective activity.

title: The Missing Half of Music History
chineseTitle: 音乐史上缺失的另一半：被遗忘的女性旋律与 AI 偏见
speaker: Gabriella Di Laccio
speakerTitle: 女高音歌唱家 · DONNE 基金会创始人
rawAdTrimmed: ✂️ 已剔除 4分12秒广告
quote: What gets heard is chosen, and those choices will shape what the future will remember.
quoteTranslation: 能被听到的声音是经过选择的，而那些选择将决定未来会记住什么。

segments.title: 开场清唱导入 (Opening Chant)
segments.original: (Singing Comtessa de Dia melody...)
segments.translation: （无伴奏高音吟唱中世纪法国女作曲家迪亚伯爵夫人的流传古旋律……）

segments.title: 900年孤独与旧书摊的震惊发现
segments.original: This song is almost 900 years old. It was written by Comtessa de Dia, a poet and composer from medieval southern France. It is the only surviving melody written by a woman from that entire tradition. So let me start with the question: who decides which voices survive? I never really thought about that until a few years ago, when I was working in a second-hand book market in London, and I found an encyclopedia that listed 6,000 women composers in the history of music. I could not believe it because at that time I think I could name five. But as soon as I started looking into their names and listening to this incredible music, I kid you not, I would not shut up. Well I haven't shut up. I'm here. And I just am sharing this music with everybody all the time. In fact, please allow me.
segments.translation: 这首歌已有将近 900 年的历史了。它是由中世纪法国南部的诗人兼作曲家迪亚伯爵夫人所作。这是那个时代完整传统中，由女性谱写的唯一流传至今的旋律。那么，请允许我以这样一个问题开始：究竟是谁在决定，哪些声音能够流传下来？直到几年前，我从未真正思考过这个问题。当时我在伦敦的一家二手旧书市场工作，偶然发现了一本百科全书，里面列出了音乐史上 6,000 位女性作曲家。我简直不敢相信，因为在那个时候，我觉得自己顶多只能说出 5 个名字。但当我开始查阅她们的名字、聆听这些令人震撼的音乐时——没骗你，我根本停不下来。好吧，到现在我也没停过，我就站在这里。我一直在不停地与所有人分享这些音乐。事实上，请允许我放一段给大家听。

segments.title: 现场乐曲赏析 (Music Interlude)
segments.original: (Music: Classical strings mixed with Afro-American romantic dance rhythms playing on stage...)
segments.translation: （现场播放音乐片段：古典弦乐融合非裔美国人浪漫舞蹈节拍……）

segments.title: 台下互动与丈夫的日常调侃
segments.original: I mean, can you believe that? Did you hear all the classical strings? The Afro-American dances mixed with the romantic music? Well welcome to my husband's life in 2018. (Laughter)
segments.translation: 我是说，你们能相信吗？你们听到那些古典弦乐了吗？融合了浪漫主义音乐的非裔美国人舞蹈节奏？好吧，欢迎体验我丈夫在 2018 年的生活状态。（笑声）

segments.title: 铁路工程师丈夫的幽默自嘲
segments.original: Now, my husband, he's a railway engineer, which means he's now the railway engineer who knows the most about women composers in the whole world. (Laughter) I know, it's not a very competitive field, but still. (Laughter)
segments.translation: 我丈夫是个铁路工程师，这意味着他现在成了全世界上最了解女性作曲家的铁路工程师。（笑声）我知道，这并不是一个竞争多么激烈的领域，但这依然很厉害。（笑声）

segments.title: 从早餐碎碎念到创立 18,000 人全球基金会
segments.original: So one day he said to me, 'Look, it's very nice that you're playing this music by these women at breakfast for like, I don't know, a year now. But you do understand that nothing is going to happen if you just tell me. I'm an engineer. So are you going to do something or what?' And I was like, 'Fair enough.' So I did. I made a list of these incredible women. I put it online, and within months, women from all over the world started writing to me and they said, 'Thank you so much for what you're doing. I'm a composer. Could you please add me to your list?' And I tell you, this list continues to grow. It is now a foundation, and we are now uncovering over 18,000 women composers in the history of music. (Applause)
segments.translation: 于是有一天他对我说：‘听着，你每天吃早餐时放这些女性作曲家的音乐，都放了大概一年了，这确实挺好。但你应该明白，只跟我讲，这个世界不会发生任何改变。我是个工程师。所以你到底打不打算做点什么？’ 我当时心想：‘说得在理。’ 于是我行动了。我为这些杰出的女性整理了一份清单发布到网上。几个月之内，全世界的女性开始给我写信：‘太感谢你的付出了。我也是一名作曲家，能把我也加进你的名单吗？’ 我告诉大家，这份名单还在不断壮大。它现在已经变成了一个基金会，我们已经在音乐史上发掘出了超过 18,000 位女性作曲家。（掌声）

segments.title: 职业音乐人的认知反思与 90% 悬殊差距
segments.original: Now this story makes absolutely no sense. I'm a professional musician. How is it possible that I spent my life training and performing without hearing about thousands of women who wrote beautiful music? Well when I started doing my own research, and I came across the data, then it became clear because, it turns out, that nearly 90 percent of the music we hear across genres is written by men. That's a very big gap. Can you imagine all the amazing music we've been all missing all this time? But also that AI is now learning from that same silence. On one platform only, more than 50,000 AI-generated tracks are added every single day. The systems can only learn from the data available to them, but right now that data is missing. Half of humanity's creativity. Now I believe musicians should be writing music, not machines. (Applause)
segments.translation: 仔细想想，这整件事根本毫无逻辑。我是一名受过专业训练的职业音乐人。我怎么可能花了一辈子在训练和演出，却从未听说过成千上万谱写出绝美旋律的女性？当我开始自己动手调研并看到真实数据时，一切真相大白：事实证明，我们在所有流派中听到的音乐里，近 90% 都是由男性创作的。这是个巨大的鸿沟。你能想象我们一直以来错过了多少动人心魄的音乐吗？更可怕的是，人工智能现在正在从这种同样的历史沉默中吸收养分。仅在某一个平台上，每天就会上传超过 50,000 首由 AI 生成的音轨。AI 系统只能从现存可用数据中学习，但眼下这些数据是残缺的——人类一半的创造力在其中缺席了。我坚信，写音乐的应该是音乐家，而不是机器。（掌声）

segments.title: 艺术伦理：未经许可与报酬使用创作是错误的
segments.original: There are millions of talented people who can do that. Writing music fills our soul ... as humans. And to generate music from artists' work without their consent or proper remuneration is wrong. (Applause and cheers)
segments.translation: 世界上有数以百万计才华横溢的人能够创作音乐。创作音乐滋养着我们作为人类的灵魂。而未经艺术家同意、不给予合理报酬，就用他们的作品来生成音乐，这是不道德的。（掌声与欢呼）

segments.title: 正视技术浪潮：通过录制让尘封作品重现光芒
segments.original: But the technology is here to stay. So let's make sure all voices are heard, right? So how do we do that? It's actually quite easy. We must record the missing voices -- the historical ones, but also the current ones who are not represented. Because a recording makes this music searchable, teachable, and part of the systems shaping what the world will hear next. It brings this music to classrooms, to radio stations, to streaming platforms so everybody in this room can play and share it.
segments.translation: 然而技术浪潮不可阻挡。所以我们必须确保所有的声音都能被听见，对吗？那我们该怎么做？其实非常简单。我们必须把那些缺失的声音录制下来——包括历史上的，也包括当下未被充分代表的声音。因为录音让这些音乐变得可检索、可教学，并成为塑造未来世界听觉系统的一部分。它能把这些作品带入教室、电台和流媒体平台，让在场的每个人都能演奏与分享。

segments.title: 向科技巨头的郑重倡议：被听见的才是被铭记的
segments.original: So here's my invitation. What if every tech company making AI music and anyone profiting from it would invest in making our musical catalog more complete? Can you imagine? What gets heard is chosen, and those choices will shape what the future will remember. So who decides which voices survive? Now more than ever, we do.
segments.translation: 因此，这是我的倡议：如果每家研发 AI 音乐的科技公司以及从中获利的各方，都能投资去完善我们的音乐馆藏，那会怎样？你能想象吗？能被听到的声音是经过选择的，而那些选择将决定未来会记住什么。那么，究竟是谁在决定哪些声音能够流传？比以往任何时候都更确定的是：决定权在我们手里。

segments.title: 集中营里埋在工具棚下的摇篮曲《Wiegala》
segments.original: And I want to leave you all with one woman's story. Ilse Weber was a poet, a singer who was imprisoned in the ghetto of Theresienstadt during World War II with her family. As she was there, she didn't write symphonies, but she wrote songs to entertain the elderly and the children. That's the power of music. And that was the gift of one woman. She and her son sadly died in Auschwitz, but her husband buried her manuscripts under a tool shed, and because of that, a few of her songs survived. This one is a lullaby. It's called 'Wiegala'.
segments.translation: 最后，我想给大家留下一个女性的故事。伊尔丝·韦伯（Ilse Weber）是一位诗人和歌唱家，二战期间她与家人一起被囚禁在特雷津集中营隔离区。在那里，她没有创作交响乐，而是写歌来抚慰老人和孩子们。这就是音乐的力量，也是一个普通女性的奉献。遗憾的是，她和儿子最终在奥斯威辛遇难，但她的丈夫把她的乐谱手稿埋在了一个工具棚下面，正因如此，她的几首歌才得以留存人世。这首是一首摇篮曲，叫作《Wiegala》。

segments.title: 历史沉默的震撼收尾与全场掌声
segments.original: (Singing 'Wiegala'...) (Song stops abruptly) [If you can't hear this part, perhaps history never recorded it.] Artificial intelligence is learning. Let's teach it to remember the sounds of all of us. Thank you. (Applause)
segments.translation: （现场演唱摇篮曲《Wiegala》……）（歌声戛然而止）[如果你听不到这一部分，也许是因为历史从未将它记录下来。] 人工智能正在学习。让我们教会它去铭记我们所有人的声音。谢谢大家。（全场热烈掌声）

spoken.quote: Now this story makes absolutely no sense. I'm a professional musician.

title: Meet the youngest-ever mayor in Japan's history
chineseTitle: 日本史上最年轻市长：以深度倾听重塑社区治理与公共信任
speaker: Ryosuke Takashima
speakerTitle: 日本芦屋市市长 · 哈佛毕业生
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Leadership is not about having all the answers from day one. It is about holding the space to listen.
quoteTranslation: 领导力并不意味着从第一天起就掌握所有答案，而是在于留出空间去真正倾听。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：Sometimes citizens think, oh, this is...
segments.original: Sometimes citizens think, oh, this is my personal problem, personal issue. So it's the kind of waste of time to speak up. But this is not true. If someone speak up and others agree with it, that personal issue becomes social issue. With my administration, the city government actually did not make a town vision. Instead of that, citizens create a vision by themselves. And we, local government, support the process. Because cities is citizens. Cities is not the government. title: How to tap into your awareness -- and why meditation is easier than you think
chineseTitle: 如何唤醒当下觉知：正念冥想远比你想象的更简单
speaker: Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche
speakerTitle: 藏传禅修导师 · 畅销书《世界上最快乐的人》作者
quote: Awareness is like the sky in the mountain, and the panic is like a storm in the mountain. No matter how strong a storm is, it does not change the nature of the sky.
quoteTranslation: 觉知就像山中的天空，而恐慌就像山间的暴风雨。无论暴风雨多么猛烈，它都无法改变天空的本质。

spoken.meaning: 开门见山、直接切入正题（在演讲与日常表达中用于迅速聚焦核心观点）
spoken.quote: What we call the essence of meditation is awareness. Knows what you are thinking, feeling, doing, seeing, hearing. That's all.
spoken.pronunciation: /kʌt tə ðə tʃeɪs/ - cut 与 to 自然弱读，chase 强摩擦音收尾。

spoken.meaning: 把某人逼疯、令人难以忍受（生动口语，表达强烈的情绪干扰）
spoken.quote: And lot of storms in the Himalayan mountains, thunderstorm, snowstorm. These storms drive me crazy.
spoken.pronunciation: /draɪv miː ˈkreɪzi/ - drive 与 me 节奏紧凑，crazy 前重后轻。

spoken.meaning: 断断续续、时断时续（形容习惯或状态未能持续坚持）
spoken.quote: I love the idea of meditation, but I don't like the practice of meditation. So on and off like that for five years.
spoken.pronunciation: /ɒn ənd ɒf/ - on 与 and 自然连读为 on-and，and 弱化为 /ənd/。

spoken.meaning: 丢面子、丢脸（东亚文化语境中的地道对译表达）
spoken.quote: I feel embarrassed to leave because I told all my childhood friends that I can do the retreat, you know. I don't want to lose my face.
spoken.pronunciation: /luːz feɪs/ - lose 末尾浊辅音 /z/ 与 face 清辅音 /f/ 对比清晰。

spoken.meaning: 买一赠二（用商业俗语幽默比喻修习觉知附带带来的慈悲与智慧）
spoken.quote: So three in one: awareness, love and compassion, wisdom. Sometimes what I call buy one, get two free. Big deal, right?
spoken.pronunciation: /baɪ wʌn, ɡɛt tuː friː/ - 充满幽默口吻，get 与 two 略有停顿强化节奏。

grammar.name: The more... the more... 比例双重比较结构
grammar.quote: The more, when you try to stop thinking what happens, you will think more. / The more you look for relax, then peace, calm, joy, relax run away.
grammar.explanation: 经典的“越……就越……”递进关联句型，在哲理阐释中用于揭示心理反作用力法则：刻意抑制念头反而强化念头。

grammar.name: No matter how + 形容词 让步状语从句
grammar.quote: And no matter how strong a storm is, it doesn't change the nature of sky.
grammar.explanation: no matter how 引导强让步，相当于 however strong a storm is，用来论证内心本质觉知的不可动摇。

grammar.name: What we call 插入性名词性从句作定语/主语
grammar.quote: What we call, when you see the river, you're out of the river. / What we call open awareness meditation.
grammar.explanation: 演讲口语中极为地道的引导标记语（discourse marker），用于引入行话或自创隐喻，相当于“也就是我们常说的”。

vocab.meaning: 惊恐发作、急性焦虑发作
vocab.detail: 临床心理学专业词汇，指突发且极度强烈的恐惧、心悸与濒死感。

vocab.meaning: 沉醉于极度极乐状态、逃避现实的狂喜
vocab.detail: 非正式英语，常指通过某种方式追求虚幻的空灵快感，在禅修中特指一种执着于平静的误区。
东方哲学与心理学中的经典隐喻，形容人心念如野猴跳跃不停、难以驯服的混乱状态。
抛弃居所、财产与身份，在无保障的漂泊流浪中磨砺心性与觉知的极高阶禅修修行。

segments.original: So, I would like to discuss about meditation, what we call the essence of meditation is awareness. And what is awareness knows what you are thinking, feeling, doing, seeing, hearing, that's all. So, actually, meditation is very easy. But many people found difficult. Why? They are too misunderstandable meditation. So, the first is many people think meditation means think of nothing. Stop thinking, concentration. I'm meditating, keep quiet. So, the more when you try to stop thinking, what happens, you will think more. So, we will do a small experiment, okay? Now, please don't think about pizza. No pizza? No pizza? What happened? Did you think about pizza? No. Yes, raise your hand. I know. So, actually, we don't need to stop thinking. We just need to connect with awareness. And another misunderstanding about meditation is what we call blazing out. Looking for peace, calm, joy, relax. The more you for relax, then peace, calm, joy, relax, and run away. So, let me share you my own experience. When I was young, I had panic attacks, although I was born in the right middle of the Himalayan mountain, the area, the village.

segments.original: How to do that? Just like listen to sound, when you listen to sound, sound becomes support for your meditation. Now you can watch panic. If you see the panic, great, what we call, when you see the river, you're out of river. When you see the mountain, you're out of mountain. So now awareness becomes more than panic, more than depression, stress, monkey mind, whatever. Let them come, let them go. So this is the first benefit. And second benefit, what we call, there's wisdom comes. So when you look at the panic, panic is not solid stone anymore. Panic become pieces, frightened image, voice, background, belief. Then if you take one of these away, you cannot find panic. So what I call panic become like shaving foam, look like piece of rock, but inside full bubbles. Then three, what I call this is acceptance, like self-kind, self-love, self-compassion. You let panic come and go, that's the real acceptance, isn't it? So three in one, awareness, love and compassion, wisdom, sometimes what I call, buy one, get true free.

title: The 60 seconds that make or break a conversation
chineseTitle: 决定职场沟通成败的关键 60 秒：T-I-P 黄金沟通框架
speaker: Chris Fenning
speakerTitle: 全球资深沟通教练 · 畅销书《The First Minute》作者
rawAdTrimmed: ✂️ 已剔除 2分08秒广告
quote: Every time we communicate, it is an opportunity to create clarity or confusion. And clarity begins from the very first minute.
quoteTranslation: 我们每一次开口沟通，都是一次创造清晰或制造混乱的机会；而真正的清晰，始于最初的第一分钟。

segments.title: 反常开场与职场低效沟通代价
segments.original: I want to be long-winded and unclear. It's not a common opening line. Most people won't tell us when they're going to be long-winded, but we know. We can tell pretty quickly if someone's going to get to the point, or if we are in for a long and painful conversation. And this is especially true at work. Every year, poor communication costs businesses hundreds of billions of dollars in lost productivity.
segments.translation: ‘我今天打算讲得冗长而含糊。’ 这可不是常见的开场白。大多数人不会事先告诉我们他们将要长篇大论，但我们心里都清楚。我们能非常敏锐地察觉出一个人是直奔主题，还是我们即将陷入一场漫长而痛苦的对话。在职场中更是如此。每年，低效糟糕的沟通都会让企业因生产力损失而付出数千亿美元的代价。

segments.title: 现场举手调查：我们是否也是那个冗长含糊的人？
segments.original: And I have to confess, the early part of my career, I was responsible for at least some of that. But I'm not alone. Hands up if you work with someone who is long-winded or unclear. That's a lot of hands. Now I'm sure we are all thinking about people outside this room, right? Except for those of you pointing at each other. But what would happen if we asked the people outside this room? They might be thinking about us.
segments.translation: 我必须坦白，在职业生涯早期，我自己至少也要为一部分损失负责。但我绝不是特例。如果在座各位有谁身边的同事说话啰嗦冗长、含糊不清的，请举手——果然有很多人举手。我现在敢肯定，大家心里想的都是这个房间以外的人，对吧？除了那几位互相指着对方的观众。但如果我们去问这个房间外面的人呢？他们可能心里想的正是在座的我们。

segments.title: 第一分钟的力量：7.5万人验证的职场法则
segments.original: And while our goal is to be clear and concise, do we really know how? Every time we communicate, we have an opportunity to create clarity or confusion, and clarity begins from the very first minute. If you get the first minute right, you set your conversation up for success. Get it wrong, your conversations will be longer, less effective and more frustrating. Now, on the off chance we could all use a little more clarity, I'm going to share a tip with you today. A tip that will help each of you improve the success of your communication at work. A tip that has been tested by more than 75,000 people around the world, and a tip that will help each of you get the first minute right.
segments.translation: 虽然我们的目标都是表达清晰精炼，但我们真的知道该怎么做吗？我们每一次沟通，都是一次创造清晰或制造混乱的机会，而真正的清晰，始于最初的第一分钟。如果你把第一分钟讲对了，你就为整场对话奠定了成功的基调；一旦搞砸了，你的对话就会变得更冗长、更低效、更令人沮丧。那么，借着我们都需要更多清晰表达的机会，我今天想和大家分享一个小技巧。这个技巧帮助了全球超过 75,000 人提升了职场沟通的成功率，也能帮助大家牢牢把握住第一分钟。

segments.title: T 代表 Topic（主题）：为什么每句话都需要明确锚点
segments.original: And here it is. There are three things we must include at the start of our work messages. And those three things begin with T, I, and P. It's a TIP. Now, the first part of the tip is the T, and T stands for topic. Every conversation at work needs a clear topic. When the topic is clear, everyone knows what we're talking about. Everyone's in sync, everybody understands. Unfortunately, reality isn't always like this, is it? How often are you in a conversation and you find yourself thinking, 'What are you talking about?' That happens when the topic is not clear.
segments.translation: 这套法则就在这里。在职场信息的开头，我们必须包含三件事，它们分别以字母 T、I、P 开头，合起来就是一个 TIP（秘诀）。秘诀的第一部分是 T，T 代表 Topic（主题）。职场中的每次对话都需要一个明确的主题。当主题清晰时，每个人都知道我们在聊什么，彼此同步，心领神会。但遗憾的是，现实往往并非如此，对吗？有多少次在对话中，你暗自思忖：‘你到底在说什么？’ 这就是主题不明确的结果。

segments.title: 亲历惨痛教训：因主题不清改错客户会议
segments.original: Now, usually the consequences are pretty minor, a little bit of wasted time, some minor frustration. But sometimes the consequences are more significant. In 2006, I was part of an engineering team writing a bid, a proposal that was worth a lot of money to our company. And a couple of days before the big meeting, my boss came up to me and said, 'Hey Chris, I need you to change the meeting from Tuesday to Thursday.' So off I went and I changed the meeting, I typed an email, sent it to the client saying, 'Something's come up, we've got to change.' And about a minute after I hit send, my phone rings. It's my boss. He had one question: 'Why did you change the meeting?' You see, he was talking about our 1-to-1. And I was thinking about the client meeting. The lack of a clear topic meant he and I were thinking about two very different things.
segments.translation: 通常情况下，后果可能并不严重，只是浪费一点时间、产生些许沮丧。但有时后果却极其沉重。2006 年，我在一个工程团队负责竞标书撰写，那份提案对我们公司价值连城。在关键汇报前几天，我的老板走过来对我说：‘嘿 Chris，帮我把会议从周二改到周四。’ 于是我立刻去改了会议，写了封邮件发给客户说：‘临时有突发情况，我们需要改期。’ 就在我点击发送一分钟后，电话响了。是我老板。他只问了一句话：‘你为什么要改会议？’ 你看，他说的是我们内部的一对一例会，而我以为他说的是客户投标会。由于缺少明确的主题，他和我想的完全是两码事。

segments.title: I 代表 Intent（意图）：大脑的选择性注意机制
segments.original: So all our messages have to begin with a clear topic. But how? It's really easy. Start your message with one sentence that names the topic you want to talk about. And the more specific, the better. You could say, 'I'd like to talk about July sales figures,' 'I want to talk about Project Everest's timeline,' or 'Can I talk about our 1-to-1 this week?' One sentence that lets your audience know what the topic is. Now having a clear topic is a great start. But it's not enough. We need the second part of the tip, which is the I. And I stands for intent. Intent is what we want the other person to do with our message. Have you ever been in a conversation and a few minutes in thought, 'Why are you telling me this?' That happens when the intent isn't clear.
segments.translation: 所以我们所有的沟通都必须以清晰的主题开篇。但具体怎么做？其实非常简单：用一句话说出你想讨论的主题，而且越具体越好。你可以说：‘我想讨论一下 7 月份的销售数据’、‘我想聊聊珠峰项目的时间表’，或者‘我能聊聊这周的一对一例会吗？’ 只要一句话，就能让听众明白主题。然而，主题明确只是一个良好的开端，这还不够。我们还需要秘诀的第二部分——I。I 代表 Intent（意图）。意图就是我们希望对方对我们所传达的信息采取什么行动。你是否曾在听人讲话几分钟后暗想：‘你为什么要跟我说这个？’ 这正是因为意图不明确。

segments.title: 选择性注意机制：告诉大脑该把信息放在哪
segments.original: Now there's a process in our brains called selective attention. And this filters incoming information and tells you what is important and what is not. And if you don't know what to do with a message, your brain says, 'Not important,' and we stop listening. At the beginning of this talk, I told you I would give you a tip that would help improve the success of your communication at work. That told your brains what to do with this information. If I hadn't done that, I could be faced with a room full of people smiling politely while all thinking, 'Why are you telling us this?'
segments.translation: 我们大脑中有一个机制叫做‘选择性注意’（selective attention）。它会过滤接收到的信息，告诉你什么是重要的、什么不重要。如果你不知道收到这段信息该干什么，你的大脑就会自动判定‘不重要’，从而停止倾听。在这场演讲的一开始，我就告诉大家我会分享一个能提升职场沟通成效的技巧。这等于提前告诉了你们的大脑该如何处理这些信息。如果我没这么做，我面对的可能就是满屋子礼貌微笑却都在心里嘀咕‘你干嘛跟我们说这些’的听众了。

segments.title: 同事 Tina 的办公室插曲：求助与倾诉的意图错位
segments.original: I got a particularly bad day, and I walked into my colleague Tina's office and I sat down with my head in my hands, and I told her how I'd messed up on an important call with a senior leader. And when I finished talking, Tina very, very helpfully said, 'Oh, why don't you try this? And maybe we can avoid this next time.' And she was giving me all sorts of advice. The more she spoke, the more frustrated I became. I didn't want her help. And that must have been quite obvious because she just put up her hands and said, 'You clearly don't want my help. So why are you here?' I said, 'I'm really sorry. I just want to get this off my chest. Can I just talk for a minute?' And like a mother talking to a small child, she rolled her eyes: 'Well, why didn't you start with that?'
segments.translation: 有一天我心情极其糟糕，走进了同事 Tina 的办公室，双手抱头坐下来，向她倾诉我在一次与高管的重要电话会议中把事情搞砸了。当我讲完后，Tina 非常热情体贴地说：‘哎呀，你为什么不试试这样做呢？也许下次就能避免。’ 她给了我各种各样的建议。可她越说，我心里就越烦躁。我根本不需要她的解决方案。这表现得显然很明显，因为她直接举起双手说：‘你显然不需要我的建议，那你来这儿干嘛？’ 我说：‘真的对不起，我只是想找人倾诉宣泄一下（get this off my chest）。能听我聊一分钟吗？’ 她像看着小孩子一样翻了个白眼：‘那你一开始怎么不说清楚？’

segments.title: 明确意图的一句话模板：提问、决断还是吐槽？
segments.original: So when you start your message, after you've given a clear topic, tell your audience what to do with it. And again, you can do this with one line: make your intent clear. If you have a question, say, 'Can I ask you a question?' If you want someone to make a decision, say, 'I'd like your help with this decision.' If you want to get something off your chest, just say, 'Is it okay if I vent for a minute?' If you tell your audience what to do with your message, not only will their brains pay more attention, you will avoid frustrating them.
segments.translation: 所以当你开口传达信息时，在交代完清晰的主题之后，告诉听众该怎么做。同样，你可以用一句话把意图讲得一清二楚：如果你想提问，就说‘我能问你个问题吗？’；如果你需要对方做决定，就说‘这件事情我需要你帮我做个决定’；如果你只是想宣泄情绪，就直说‘我能跟你吐槽/宣泄一分钟吗？’ 只要你告诉了对方该如何处理你的信息，不仅他们的大脑会更专注，你也能避免彼此产生无谓的沮丧。

segments.title: P 代表 Point（核心要点）：童年坐车与职场‘快讲重点’
segments.original: This is where we need the third part of the tip, the P. And P stands for point. Point is the most important part of our message. If you only had five seconds to speak, it's what you would say. And usually, it's what your audience cares about the most. When I was a kid, my dad played a game with me. If we were going on a journey, I'd go, 'Dad, where are we going?' And he'd say, 'Oh, well, first, we're going to the car, and then we'll get in the car, and then we'll leave the driveway, and we'll turn left onto the main street...' I just wanted to scream, 'Where are we going?!' I wanted the short version. But fast forward a few years, I was doing the same thing at work. Someone would ask me a question, and I would give all the details, step by step information. And quite often, people would say, 'Chris, just get to the point.'
segments.translation: 接下来就是秘诀的第三部分——P。P 代表 Point（核心要点）。要点是整段信息中最重要的部分。如果你只有 5 秒钟的时间发言，这就是你应该说的那句话；而且这通常也是听众最关心的核心。小时候，我父亲经常和我玩一个游戏。每次出门旅行我都会问：‘爸爸，我们要去哪儿？’ 他就会说：‘哦，首先我们要走到车旁，然后上车，把车倒出车道，左转上主干道……’ 我当时简直想抓狂大喊：‘我们到底要去哪儿？！’ 我想要的是结论！可快进到几年后，我在工作中居然也在做一模一样的事。别人问我一个问题，我就把所有细节、前因后果一五一十全盘托出。很多时候同事都会忍不住打断：‘Chris，直接讲重点吧。’

segments.title: BLUF 原则：把结论与底线放在最前面
segments.original: And we can do this quite simply, as the military likes to say, put the bottom line up front (BLUF). In one sentence, deliver the most important piece of information: 'I want to give a refund for a late delivery,' 'Our project launch is going to be delayed by a month.' Say the most important thing, and your audience will know where that conversation is going, and they won't be thinking, 'What is your point?' If you start your conversation with topic, intent, and point, you're starting with a clear and concise introduction that answers the three questions we all have: What are you talking about? Why are you telling me this? And what is your point?
segments.translation: 我们可以非常简单地做到这一点，正如军方常说的法则：‘把底线与结论放在最前面’（BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front）。用一句话交付最重要的信息核心：‘我建议为这次延迟交货提供全额退款’、‘我们的项目上线需要推迟一个月’。先说最核心的事，你的听众立刻就能心领神会，再也不会暗自困惑‘你到底想表达什么’。如果你以主题（Topic）、意图（Intent）和核心要点（Point）开启对话，你就拥有了一个清晰利落的开场，直接解答了每个人内心的三大终极疑问：你在聊什么？干嘛跟我说？以及结论是什么？

segments.title: 终极挑战与第一分钟的魔力
segments.original: So I have a challenge for you. The next time you start a conversation at work, the next time you write a message, take a moment, and think to yourself: What is my topic? What do I intend for the other person to do with this message? And what point do I want to deliver? Imagine working somewhere where everybody did this. Imagine if everyone always knew what to do with the message you gave them, or understood what it was about. How much smoother, how much easier would our jobs be? That, ladies and gentlemen, is the power of the first minute. Thank you.
segments.translation: 因此，我想向大家发起一个挑战：下一次当你在工作中开启一段对话、或者写一封信息时，请停顿片刻，在脑海中问自己三个问题：我的主题是什么？我期望对方收到信息后采取什么行动？我最核心的结论是什么？想象一下，如果在某个工作环境中每个人都践行这一原则，如果每个人都能在第一时间秒懂彼此的意图与结论，我们的工作将会变得多么顺畅、多么轻松！女士们、先生们，这就是第一分钟的魔力。谢谢大家！

spoken.meaning: 直奔主题 / 讲重点（职场沟通核心表达）
spoken.pronunciation: /ɡet tuː ðə pɔɪnt/ - to 轻读，point 尾音干脆利落。
spoken.quote: We can tell pretty quickly if someone's going to get to the point.

spoken.meaning: 倾诉心事 / 吐露心中的苦闷与压力
spoken.pronunciation: /ɡet ðɪs ɔːf maɪ tʃest/ - off my 连贯自然。
spoken.quote: I'm really sorry. I just want to get this off my chest. Can I just talk for a minute?

spoken.meaning: 抱有一线希望 / 借着……的机会（谦逊客气的引申转折）

segments.title: 第 2 幕：So when I write a book like State of ...
segments.original: So when I write a book like State of Wonder, I'm putting an enormous energy into the construction of sets and costumes. I'm making the trees. I'm picking the birds. I'm making this world that is very far away from my world. I'm doing a lot of research. In this book, I am saying, okay, Daphne has a father and two stepfathers. So do I. Not the same father, not the same two stepfathers, but I at least understand that dynamic. And I'm, I'm going to borrow that. So there are a lot of elements that are from my life, but this is not about my life. I think though the thing that gives the book the autobiographical feel, it's dedicated to my friend Jim Fox, who died just over two years ago on his 80th birthday. And it, Jim is not Eddie. I am not Daphne. And Jim certainly was not my stepfather. He was my lawyer. But the love that we had and the friendship that we had is very much the love and the friendship that Daphne and Eddie had. And it really was a sense of like, I've lost one of my very best friends. I still have all of this love. Like where can I put it? What do you do with all of those happy memories and just joy and to put it into a book, into a narrative, and I think it does make the book feel very autobiographical? Yeah, this was such a sweeping love story in a lot of ways, but it was a platonic love story. So I'd love to know why you decided to write this kind of story between two characters. Because I feel it all the time in my life. I love the friendships in my life. And I love the ways in which friendships can be so romantic. They can be so warm and close and intertwined and funny and full of acceptance without any of the anxiety of romance. If like, are they going to go to bed together? Are they going to portray one another? Is something terrible going to pull them apart? It's just like all of the good stuff and none of the anxious stuff. And the scenes of them walking around New York and talking about life and their dreams and what they wanted to do and what they did and what they remember. It's so romantic and it was such a pleasure to write because nothing bad is going to happen. Yeah, yeah. You said recently on NPR that the former stepfather, Eddie, his words to the young Daphne when she was young shaped her whole life and similar words shaped yours too. There were apparently some nuns who told you something similar about decency that Eddie shared with Daphne. segments.translation: So when I write a book like State of Wonder, I'm putting an enormous energy into the construction of sets and costumes. I'm making the trees. I'm picking the birds. I'm making this world that is very far away from my world. I'm doing a lot of research. In this book, I am saying, okay, Daphne has a father and two stepfathers. So do I. Not the same father, not the same two stepfathers, but I at least understand that dynamic. And I'm, I'm going to borrow that. So there are a lot of elements that are from my life, but this is not about my life. I think though the thing that gives the book the autobiographical feel, it's dedicated to my friend Jim Fox, who died just over two years ago on his 80th birthday. And it, Jim is not Eddie. I am not Daphne. And Jim certainly was not my stepfather. He was my lawyer. But the love that we had and the friendship that we had is very much the love and the friendship that Daphne and Eddie had. And it really was a sense of like, I've lost one of my very best friends. I still have all of this love. Like where can I put it? What do you do with all of those happy memories and just joy and to put it into a book, into a narrative, and I think it does make the book feel very autobiographical? Yeah, this was such a sweeping love story in a lot of ways, but it was a platonic love story. So I'd love to know why you decided to write this kind of story between two characters. Because I feel it all the time in my life. I love the friendships in my life. And I love the ways in which friendships can be so romantic. They can be so warm and close and intertwined and funny and full of acceptance without any of the anxiety of romance. If like, are they going to go to bed together? Are they going to portray one another? Is something terrible going to pull them apart? It's just like all of the good stuff and none of the anxious stuff. And the scenes of them walking around New York and talking about life and their dreams and what they wanted to do and what they did and what they remember. It's so romantic and it was such a pleasure to write because nothing bad is going to happen. Yeah, yeah. You said recently on NPR that the former stepfather, Eddie, his words to the young Daphne when she was young shaped her whole life and similar words shaped yours too. There were apparently some nuns who told you something similar about decency that Eddie shared with Daphne. I went to Catholic Girl School for 12 years and there were nuns and one in particular, Sister Nina, 94 still very, very much in my life. But the idea that you're part of a collective and that you are not ever one voice. It's like you all sing together and you shouldn't necessarily know where your voice is. Yeah. And the message about kindness, I think the words where people are kind and your job is to be kind in our town. Oh, yeah. The people are generally good and decent and we should trust them and there's like a small percentage of people that we might need to fear but we don't need to design our lives around that. And I thought that was a really powerful message. Yes. And it makes me so sad actually. I lived down the street from a school and it's a boys school. And in the morning and I'm walking the dogs and the boys are walking to school. And you say good morning to them and they look at the ground because they've all been trained to not talk to strangers. The most important thing is that you don't engage with anybody you don't know as a method of keeping yourself safe. And I understand. I mean, I understand terrible things happen. But for every one terrible thing that happens, a million good things happen. And if you cut yourself off from the potential of the terrible thing, you're also cutting yourself off from the potential of just the kindness of daily interaction and the warmth of connecting with other people and their dogs when you're out there.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：Yeah
segments.original: Yeah. Yeah. And so many people listening have been curious about the title of this book and the story of the horse on the cover. Okay. So the book is called Whistler. And Whistler is a horse and Whistler the horse is on the cover of the book. Whistler is what we call a bay. So sort of a chestnut brown and she has a couple of white stockings and a white place. And she is standing in a field in Wyoming. There's a night sky behind her. She's got on her saddle. Her bridle is hanging down and it's because the horse is run away. And then three days later, the horse has come back. And it was very important to me that the horse be looking out at the viewer. And when Noah Satterstrom painted this painting, I said, can you make the horse look straight ahead? And he said the eyes are on the side of their head. It's really hard to make a horse look straight ahead. And I said, Hey, figure it out. And he did. It looks great. But this is not a book about a horse. If you don't like books about horses, you're going to really like this book. And if you long for another book about a horse, you're going to be really disappointed. The horse is on maybe five pages of the book. But the horse who is not hurt, that's the other thing that I have to remember to say, people really want to know the horse is okay through the whole book. But the horse is in a story that Eddie tells to Daphne when they are in a perilous car accident and trapped overnight in a car. And he's trying to tell her a story to take her mind off their circumstances. And the story that he tells her was from a book proposal that he had read just that afternoon. He is in publishing. And it turns out to be a story that is way too scary and stressful for a nine year old. But he doesn't understand that. And he gets into the middle of the story. And he desperately wants to get out of it. And he's like, I'll tell you the end later when we're out of the car. And she's like, no, you will tell me the story of what happens with Whistler now. But the thing is Whistler comes back. And Whistler is emblematic of all that is loyal and true. And in as the novel progresses, Daphne comes to think of Eddie as Whistler and Eddie comes to think of Daphne as Whistler. So the horse just stands in the place of love and loyalty. But somebody said to me a couple of weeks ago, this looks like the kind of book, a fifth grade girl who is crazy about horses would want to buy. And I thought that's exactly what I was going for. That old fashion horse book like Black Beauty or Black Stallion. But in this one, the horse isn't hurt. And there isn't a terrible ending. But it is the kind of book that or the kind of cover that Daphne would have liked when she was a little girl. And Eddie was in her life. Yeah. As a parent. And of course, as a daughter, I also found myself really resonating with the exploration of parenting in the book. This is a theme in some of your other books as well. So I want to acknowledge that. But why did you want to take on this theme of looking back in time and sort of reassessing our relationships with our parents and reassessing our parents themselves as human beings as we age? And we become, you know, fully grown up. Right. Well, let's go back to the aforementioned sister Nina, my nun who taught me to read in first through third grade. And I hated her. I missed a ton of school in those years. We moved around a lot. I wandered in and out of the classroom. I did not become a comfortable reader until I was in the third grade. And sister Nina stayed on me, kept me in from recess for years because she thought it was important that I learned how to read and I hated her for it. All right. There is my assessment that I made of this woman when I was six years old at six. I I decided she was a bad person who was really mean. But the interesting thing is, I kept that assessment throughout my adult life so that when people would tell their bad nun stories, I would always be like, Oh, you should have met this nun that I had when I was a kid.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：She kept me in from research research...
segments.original: She kept me in from research research, recess every day and probably research. And then when I was 39, she called me out of the blue. And she was working at a St Vincent DePaul school down and she said, we've got nothing. We don't have paper. We don't have scissors. We don't have glue sticks. There was just a super poor school. She said, we need money. I have been following your career. I know you have money. I want you to give me some money so that we can buy school supplies. And I said, sure. And this happened a couple of times. And then I said, listen, let's get together. And she was living in a condo at the time with some other nuns who were still teaching because the rest of them had all been shipped off to the old nuns home. And when I got there, she was standing out in the parking lot. And she's like, four 11 and weighs 80 pounds. It is Italian. And I got out of the car. And she's she's standing there holding out her arms to me. And I thought, this woman doesn't hate me. This woman was never on time to me. This woman only wanted to teach me to read. And I have held a grudge against her all this time. And I took that energy, that scenario. And I gave it to Daphne and her mother. So Daphne is incredibly angry at her mother when she is nine years old because Abigail Daphne's mother is divorcing Eddie. Daphne can't stand this. It's unfair. And she really breaks with her mother. And as she becomes an adult, she still is distant and cold to her mother because she's still angry. And over the course of the novel, she has the chance to really see as an adult what her mother was struggling with with both her first husband and her second husband and her third husband in a different way. And and Daphne can finally see her mother as a human being. And it's not that Daphne forgives her mother. It's that Daphne comes to understand there was nothing to forgive. Oh, so powerful. And when you my mind just wandered when you mentioned the third husband too, because I want to acknowledge how hilarious he was, the positively positive guy. Was anyone the inspiration for that? I was just curious. I mean, if you want to do a little peek behind the curtain. Yes, absolutely. And I was doing a podcast with Adam Grant. And he was like, are you making fun of people who write self-help books? And I said, oh no, I am making fun of myself. I mean, I am Lucas Ecker. I am the person who's always positive. And people are making fun of me, because I am a Pollyanna. And I am the one who's like, things are going to turn out. Like, I know this is a really hard time in the world. I know this is a hard time in human history, in the history of our country, but I have complete confidence in the basic goodness of human beings. And I think that we're all going to get through this. And my friends are like, oh, God, would you give it a rest? Well, we love that about you. And that's why that's why we need you. That's why I you're a treasure. Yeah, but I can be quite tiresome too.

segments.title: 第 5 幕：And I'd love to move to craft for a m...
segments.original: And I'd love to move to craft for a moment because so many questions from our listeners came in about craft. I thought we could start with a scene from Whistler that really stood out to me or an exchange, a dialogue exchange. Daphne is speaking with her sister, who's a psychologist. And she says something like, who remembers what happens to you when you're nine. And her sister says, that's all we ever remember. And it speaks to kind of how frozen our childhoods can feel this harkens back to your example too of how you thought about sister Nina. Can you walk us through your writing practice and how you go through planning out an exchange like this or keeping track of the dialogue such that it feels so real, because that's something that really resonates with so many of your readers and fans. I don't plan it out. I mean, I plan out the larger structure of the book. And I do know what the arc is and where I'm going. But I don't sketch out a scene. I pretty much just write it. And it's all about knowing who these people are. If you understand who the characters are, it's like improv. Then you can speak in their voice. You know what Lita's going to say, you know what Daphne is going to say, I understand who they are. And then I drop them into a particular moment. And then I can type. And then as far as getting the language right or the sentences, I always say, this is what I do for a living. So I had a whole lifetime of working on this, how to listen and and knowing the difference between speech and dialogue. When I was young, I once dated a guy who worked in the district attorney's office. And he would have wire taps and we would read wire taps for hours and hours. And boy, nothing taught me more about how to write dialogue than to read 600 pages of wiretaps of a phone. It's unbelievably boring what people say to one another. And the ability to pick out a single sentence or half sentence. And we have them together, so that you are encompassing big ranging ideas in a few sentences. That's dialogue. Yeah, well, you're so good at it. Ted member, Anka, A asks, how do you decide which moments in a character's life deserve the spotlight and which moments are best left for the readers to imagine? You know, it's again going back to just knowing them. And I could have picked different moments that would have been emblematic. It's just not picking too many of them or having too many of them that are boring. You want to kind of just drop in, drill down briefly, make sure that you have a good picture of the scene, even if you're thinking about Henry James. You know, even if you're thinking about a novel like Wings of the Dove, which is 800 pages. And there are some long, slow scenes in there. But there may be 20 or 30 pages. And then he is going on to another moment, another moment. Even Henry James isn't giving us every single turn of the character. There's, there's just editing. Do you feel like your sense of taste or your filter as an author comes from getting bored easily with yourself? Like do you have a lower threshold for what's exciting? Just the opposite.

segments.title: 第 6 幕：I think I have one of the highest thr...
segments.original: I think I have one of the highest thresholds for boring around. I mean, to wit, I read a lot of Henry James. I can really stick with things that are very slow and very quiet. And also, my husband always says, I have the opposite of attention deficit disorder. I have attention surplus disorder. Leave me in a room. And I can just stay on on point focused for an entire day. And my idea of a great adventure is reading Prused in a hard-back cherry. You know, just saying really focused on one thing. So it's no, it's not that I have a short attention span. It's not even that I am writing to cater to a short attention span. It goes back to reading wiretaps. It's just that I understand that if you want to get something across, you can't do it by giving every single detail. For example, my real stepfather, who was a neuro-autologist, he dealt with a very specific kind of brain tumor between the ear and the brain. But he wanted to be a novelist. And he wrote huge novels practically every other month that he would then wind and give to me. It was both abusive and really so instructive. But if he had a character who was going in to take a shower, which for no reason didn't figure into the story whatsoever, what the character would go in would turn on the faucet, would adjust the heat, the cold, hold back the shower curtain, check the soap, undress, make sure there was a towel. I was like, oh, it would take 10 pages. And the shower didn't take sense of in a horror film or something like that. Like a lot of attention. Anything about the character, it didn't move the plot forward in any way. And I really do think we can learn so much more by seeing people fail than by seeing them succeed. So I would read check off and think, well, I mean, I'm never going to be able to do that. I can't even imagine how check off did that. But I could read my stepfather's novels, thousands and thousands of pages I read throughout my youth. And I said, oh, I am never doing that. Again, it's a wiretap situation. That's why I think actually going to MFA programs can be really helpful because you can see the people in your class doing things wrong. And you're like, well, that's a sinkhole that I don't want to walk into. And you can learn more quickly sometimes than you can if you're just watching everybody do everything perfectly. Yeah. Yeah. You have said that writing about kindness and gentleness takes more craft than writing about darkness. Why? Well, think about it. You've got a picnic. And in that picnic, a terrible tornado blows up and sweeps half the family away. And the rest of them are up in a tree. And you know, there's action. There's action generated by disaster. But if you're having a picnic of kind people who are talking in a civil way and enjoying their lunch, then you have to really think about what is the tension in the scene and what are these people actually saying to one another and how can I move the story along? One of the things that I've thought about so much in the last just couple of years is complaining anger, bitterness, frustration, it's low hanging fruit. And just to walk in and say, oh, it's terrible. It's just never, never been worse to which I always say, did you read about the children's crusades? Did you read about the plague? This is not the worst moment in human history.

segments.title: 第 7 幕：And climb up the tree a little bit fa...
segments.original: And climb up the tree a little bit farther and see what you can say about what's positive. It's not that you're ignoring what's negative, but put something good out there in the world. I used to do a lot of travel writing. And every now and then I would get sent off on a cruise. And somebody who was an editor at Travel and Leisure said to me, we only send the very best writers on cruises because nothing happens. And are you able to write an essay about a cruise ship in which nothing happens? Well, this reminds me of David Foster Wallace, right? I suppose the leading thing that I'll never do again is about a cruise. I was just going to say exactly that. Yeah, they sent the very best writer of all on a cruise. And that piece is riveting in which all he's trying to do is figure out how he can make it back to his cabin to catch the person who is cleaning because he never sees the person who is cleaning. Like that's the tension. And that's the answer. That's the answer. It takes a lot more skill to write about something where seemingly nothing is happening. And he did it better than anybody. Yeah, I love that essay. So listeners, if you haven't read it yet, please do. Yeah, I love all of his essays actually. Same thing. Yes, the lobster. segments.original: And I was like, that's the most horrible thing I've ever heard. And I have thought about it so much since then. And that it actually is a really beautiful thing to say. Like you can be with somebody and really love them. And I have a very successful relationship. And it is not a relationship you will have forever. And that doesn't mean that it was a failure. And you don't need to frame it as a failure. But how have I evolved? How is my writing evolved? I think it goes back to that idea of set design that I used to feel it was so important that no one knew anything about my life that I was writing things that appeared to be strictly from my imagination. When in fact, everything is from your life. If you're writing science fiction about little green Martians with suction cup toes, you know, that's your cousin, that's your sister, that's your neighbor. And to kind of come to peace with that, I've come to realize that I cannot control how people read my work. And if people are going to read it and think, oh, well, that's very autobiographical or clearly she's writing about herself. I can't go around saying, no, no, that's not what I'm writing about. No, no, that's not what this means. It's just like I'm going to write the best book I can write with the tools that I have and leave it and go on. To the literary landscape and just books in general, which is how you've connected with so many people, including me, in your talk you said, I've come to believe that if you're interested in living in a society where people read, it's also your responsibility to cultivate readers. This is foundational, but just to set the table here, why do we need a society where people read? Okay, this is just me, this is just, you know, the way I see society, but I think that reading and the telling of stories is how we, as mammals, communicate, this is what the human animal does. We shape our experience into stories. At the end of the day my husband will come home and he'll say, what did you do today? And I will say, oh, I did a podcast with a lease from Ted and we had a really long tech check and I had to get the cameras set up just right. And I was wearing a white shirt and I changed to a black, you know, I will make it into a story of this experience. And I will try to make it entertaining and I'll try to make it funny. And then he will tell me about being a doctor and patients that he saw. And this is how we exchange bits of our day and this is how we stay connected. And to my way of thinking, reading and books are so central to that activity because it allows us to connect to the people that we've never met. And you can say, oh, you can do that on the internet too. You can do that on social media, but I think that there is a depth and a thoughtfulness that comes from writing these stories down and then sending them out into the world and everyone having their own experiences with the stories and then coming together. That's the crazy thing because reading is such a solitary activity.

segments.title: 第 9 幕：And yet I've owned a bookstore for 15...
segments.original: And yet I've owned a bookstore for 15 years and I am out on this giant book tour right now. And every night all these people show up. And they show up because they want to talk about my book, but also because they want to talk to each other and connect to other people as readers. And it's an incredible point of connection that I feel like now more than ever we need. I'm glad that you brought up the bookstore because you really serve as a model for what it means to be a literary citizen with all of the work that you do outside of writing. What are you proudest of right now? I definitely feel like I've done more for the state of the humanities in this country as a bookseller than I have as a writer. And part of that is having author events, having this social media through the bookstore, which is weird because I'm actually not on social media, but the bookstore is. And so I'm always holding up books twice a week and talking about books that I love, which has been a great means of not only making recommendations of books that are brand new and books that are old and you might have forgotten about, but to promote a conversation around books. So that's part of it. The Pernaz's foundation, which is not mine or me. It is something that the bookstore came up with and we've all really worked on together as a team. We buy books for children in Title I schools. And so we can bring in authors and illustrators who would normally go to private schools or fancy public schools because the financial model for writers and illustrators going into schools is that the parents of the children have to order the books in advance. Now they don't have to because we can buy all of the books and give every kid in the class a free book. And then something else that I have been involved with for 10 years is the book industry charitable foundation, which is called BINK. And we make emergency grants to people who work in book and mortar bookstores. And that is an amazing, amazing organization. So if you are working in a bookstore and your car breaks and your kid gets sick and you have to miswork for a couple of weeks, there was one bookseller I met once who said BINK came through when I needed the money to pay for my mother's funeral. So many people are a couple of thousands of dollars between being okay and not being okay. Natural disasters, fires and floods and hurricanes and displaced booksellers and booksellers who want to go back to school, BINK is there for them as well. So I spend a lot of my time now with a more tolls and we raise money for BINK so that there will be money for booksellers who need just a little bit of bridge. And you know, you can't solve all the problems, but every now and then you can help with a couple of them. And you have said that one of the most surprising things about owning a bookstore is that reading ends up being this powerful mode of connection as you have spoken about in this interview. So I'm curious after 15 years now of being a bookseller, what's the most powerful example of connection that you've seen through reading?
