title: Who controls your city's money?
chineseTitle: 谁掌握着你所在城市的财政命脉？公共银行与社区金融革命
speaker: Trinity Tran
speakerTitle: 公共银行运动倡导者 · TED Fellow
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Public banks keep public dollars working for public good, not private extraction.
quoteTranslation: 公共银行让纳税人的钱服务于公共福祉，而非沦为华尔街私人资本的掠夺工具。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：a community wants to build like a bri...
segments.original: a community wants to build like a bridge or transit system, housing, sustainable infrastructure, where does the money come from? Money ultimately decides what gets built, money decides what survives, money decides what future becomes possible. There change where money goes and who controls it, then you change what becomes possible. I'm Trinity Tran. I lead efforts to build public banks in California and beyond. Most of the time, our cities don't have the money upfront to be able to pay for a project like a bridge or housing. And so they will issue a bond, which is essentially a long term loan provided by structured by Wall Street banks. A loan is money that is provided up front and paid back over time with interest. Wall Street banks private lenders end up tacking on fees to structure and sell those bonds. Then the reality is that our local governments are not only paying for the cost of the project, but decades of interest on top of that. So for every dollar that we're borrowing, we're paying another dollar in interest over time, sometimes more. And that's all money that's going out the door to private lenders. We're paying hundreds of millions of dollars in the city of Los Angeles at the state level in California. We're paying four billion dollars in interest annually. That's money flowing out of our communities rather than being invested locally. Private banks are owned by shareholders. They're investing in areas that make them a lot of money and not necessarily what's in the best interest in our communities. Public banking asks a different question. How do we do more with the dollars that our communities generate without raising taxes? But by lowering the cost of financing itself. A public bank is a bank owned by the people through their local government, either city, or region, or state. Every time you, for instance, buy something like a cup of coffee, a portion of that tax will go to your city and your state. So we're using the money that we already generate that belongs to us. They don't have shareholders to pay. So that as loans are repaid, it comes back into a public bank. Its mission is to support the local economic development of the community it serves. That would be designed at a local level so that while that we created the California Public Banking Act, creating the legal framework for cities and municipalities to be able to form their own banks. And so the mission of the bank, the mandates, the lending priorities, investment priorities, the capitalization strategies, all the details of how this is going to work is going to be defined at a local level.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：There are 900 public banks globally
segments.original: There are 900 public banks globally. With nearly $50 trillion in assets. In Germany, a network of 400 municipal banks was able to support the country's renewable energy transition. In the United States, we have a successful model to emulate. The Bank of North Dakota is a 100-year-old public bank founded in 1919. It was started by socialist farmers who were being gouged by out-of-state New York bankers. During the Great Depression, nearly 200,000 farms were being foreclosed on. Because the state of North Dakota had a public bank, it was able to step in and buy the farms and lent it back to the families for $1. Once the families were able to stabilize, they sold it back at a price they could afford. For the last century, it has supported local economic developments, supported small businesses, infrastructure, while still returning very healthy return on equity 15% to 18%. That means it's returning hundreds of millions of dollars back into the general fund year after year. So that's an example of how a public bank is able to step in and support in strength in the community without focusing on just purely profit. Los Angeles just dealt with a devastating wildfire. So if we had a public bank, it would have been able to step in to offer immediate low-cost loans. It's able to be immediately responsive to the needs of the community without having to wait for federal aid, which can be unstable. We're moving towards a building a system that mobilizes public revenue to support our public priorities. We've seen such an incredible amount of progress in such a short time, because even without a complex understanding of finance and banking, when you start explaining public banking, it makes sense on a logical and intuitive level. Multiple cities and states are working towards it. We have the ability to create a new system. This isn't a pie-in-the-sky idea. This is a model that works for the people, our communities, and our environment. That was Trinity Tran coming up a special conversation between Trinity and Ted Fellow's program director, Lily James Olds, where they discussed the unlikely path that led Trinity into the world of banking. Trinity also talks about the central, public bank in the U.S. that's more profitable than many well-known private banks, and what it would actually take to build one where you live. Hey, Yaddies, this is Nick and Jack from the Best One Yet podcast. Now, the last company we worked at, they used pay-locity, and everything just worked.

I had never really heard anyone play accordion in this way before, and Maria explained that it's not a commonly taught instrument in the United States. spoken.meaning: 超级马里奥效应（游戏化抗挫力）
spoken.quote: In gaming, when you fall in a pit, you don't give up in shame; you simply press restart to try again.
spoken.pronunciation: Super Mario Effect 语气轻松诙谐。

spoken.meaning: 将过程游戏化 / 融入趣味挑战
spoken.quote: When you gamify the learning process, failure stops being a stain on your self-worth.
spoken.pronunciation: gamify /ˈɡeɪmɪfaɪ/ 重音在第一音节。

grammar.name: Not only ... but ... 递进倒装句
grammar.quote: Not only did participants solve the coding puzzle faster, but they also enjoyed every painful minute.
grammar.explanation: 句首 Not only 倒装引出实验惊人数据，突出心态转变带来的生产力飞跃。

vocab.detail: 心理学中坚信能力可以通过刻意练习与复盘不断拓展的心智信念。
指传统教育中由于过度严厉的打分与责难导致大脑自发规避尝试的负面心理。

title: Is AI turning us all into the same person?
chineseTitle: AI 正在把我们所有人变成同质化的单一面孔吗？
speaker: Sandra Matz
speakerTitle: 哥伦比亚大学商学院副教授 · 行为计算科学家
quote: If we let algorithms optimize away our friction and weirdness, we don't just lose our individuality -- we lose the very serendipity that drives human culture forward.
quoteTranslation: 如果我们任由算法优化掉内心的冲突与独特的怪癖，我们失去的不仅是个性，更是推动人类文化向前发展的不可预知的机缘。

spoken.meaning: 不落窠臼、偏僻少有人走的路（比喻脱离主流推荐的独特选择）
spoken.quote: Stray too far into the unknown and you might starve. But never go off the beaten track, and you miss out on new discoveries.
spoken.pronunciation: /ɔːf ðə ˈbiːtn træk/ - beaten 中 /t/ 产生鼻音爆破，track 发音短促清脆。

spoken.meaning: 以……为代价（论述技术便利与个性丧失的经典表达）
spoken.quote: We gain instant convenience, but often at the expense of our own authentic curiosity.
spoken.pronunciation: /æt ði ɪkˈspɛns əv/ - the 与 expense 自然连读 /ðiː ɪk-/, of 弱化为 /əv/。

spoken.meaning: 双刃剑（形象描述算法精准推荐带来的利与弊）
spoken.quote: Algorithmic personalization is a double-edged sword: it saves time while quietly narrowing our horizon.
spoken.pronunciation: /ə ˌdʌbl ɛdʒd sɔːrd/ - double-edged 的 /dʒd/ 与 sword 的 /s/ 需自然衔接过渡。

spoken.meaning: 死板归类、将……套入刻板印象标签
spoken.quote: The system tries to pigeonhole us into predictable taste clusters based on our past clicks.
spoken.pronunciation: /ˈpɪdʒɪnhoʊl ˈɪntuː/ - pigeon 与 hole 合成连贯，重音在第一音节。

grammar.name: The more... the more... 比例递进句型
grammar.quote: The more predictable our choices become, the more homogeneous the content ecosystem grows.
grammar.explanation: 经典的比例从句，强化算法闭环反馈带来的系统性趋同。

grammar.name: Not only... but also... 倒装与强调结构
grammar.quote: Not only does AI anticipate what we might like, but it also actively shapes what we are capable of desiring.
grammar.explanation: Not only 位于分句前引导助动词 does 倒装，增强演讲论辩力量。

vocab.detail: 指推荐算法不断根据大众热度收敛内容偏好，导致全社会审美与思维趋于单一的现象。

vocab.meaning: 认知偶然机缘 / 意外发现的惊喜
vocab.detail: 指人在没有预设目的的漫步或跨界探索中偶得新灵感的能力，常与算法过滤泡对立。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：People worry about AI for all kinds o...
segments.original: People worry about AI for all kinds of reasons. It's polarizing, it spreads misinformation, it's coming for our jobs, and those are all good reasons to be nervous. But what really keeps me up at night is something else, something that feels more personal and perhaps even more concerning for the human experience itself. I worry that AI will make us boring. You, me, all of us. That's because the more we outsource our decisions to AI, the more we surrender something deeply human, our capacity to explore, to take risks to stumble into the unknown and sometimes surprise even ourselves. I worry that without the potential for discovery, for serendipity, we risk becoming more shallow and unidimensional versions of who we are and who we could be, not just as humans, as individuals, but as humanity. Now, let me make this idea a bit more concrete and take you somewhat perhaps unexpected, but also totally relatable. Imagine walking into a Boskin Robbins. What you'll see is an illustrious assortment of 31 different ice cream flavors. There's chocolate chip, there's daschio almond, lemon sorbet, and many more. You're now facing a difficult choice. Are you going to go with an old favorite chocolate maybe? Or are you going to take a risk on something funky new, like wild and reckless sherbet?

title: Why you need the growth mindset of a weed
chineseTitle: 为什么我们需要像杂草一样拥抱野蛮生长的成长型思维
speaker: Stephen Nobles
speakerTitle: 知名教育创新者 · 终身学习实践导师
quote: A weed is just a plant whose virtues have not yet been discovered. It thrives in the cracks where nothing else is expected to grow.
quoteTranslation: 所谓杂草，不过是尚未被发现独特价值的植物。它恰恰能在无人期待生机的瓦砾缝隙中顽强绽放。

spoken.meaning: 在夹缝中茁壮成长（形容在恶劣或匮乏环境下迸发出的顽强生命力）
spoken.quote: Weeds don't ask for permission; they simply thrive in the cracks of concrete sidewalks.
spoken.pronunciation: /θraɪv ɪn ðə kræks/ - thrive 咬舌发音 /θ/，in 与 the 弱读连缀。

spoken.meaning: 透过数据看本质 / 超越冰冷指标看活生生的人
spoken.quote: As educators, our greatest responsibility is to see our students beyond the test scores and data.
spoken.pronunciation: /siː bɪˈjɒnd ðə ˈdeɪtə/ - beyond 弱读，data 发音清晰。

spoken.meaning: 冲破一切艰难险阻、出人意料地成功
spoken.quote: When you cultivate resilient curiosity, young people achieve breakthroughs against all odds.
spoken.pronunciation: /əˈɡɛnst ɔːl ɒdz/ - against 与 all 自然连读为 against-all。

grammar.name: It is not until ... that ... 强调句型
grammar.quote: It is not until we challenge our deficit mindset that genuine transformation begins.
grammar.explanation: 强调句结构，凸显摒弃“匮乏偏见”才是教育与个人成长的关键转折点。

vocab.meaning: 匮乏视角 / 缺陷取向思维
vocab.detail: 教育学与社会心理学概念，指习惯于将注意力放在个体的短板或环境缺陷，而非其潜能与韧性。

vocab.meaning: 适应性复原力 / 逆境生长力
vocab.detail: 指不仅能抵御创伤，更能主动根据环境变化重塑自身生态的终身韧性。

title: How I’m helping thousands rebuild their lives after prison
chineseTitle: 走出铁窗后的重生之路：帮助数千名刑释女性重塑尊严
speaker: Susan Burton
speakerTitle: A New Way of Life 创始人 · 人权倡导者
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Healing begins when we offer open doors, warm beds, and unconditional dignity instead of slamming cages.
quoteTranslation: 治愈始于我们为迷途者推开温暖的大门与尊严的怀抱，而非重重合上冰冷的铁窗。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：October 4th, 1997, I walked into a ro...
segments.original: October 4th, 1997, I walked into a room unlike any room I'd ever entered before. People were standing up sharing their stories. A wave of relief watched over me, I got a couple coffee and just took everything in. At that point, I was at the lowest point of my life. I was out of ideas and I didn't know how I was going to make it out of the condition I was in. Before that date, my life had not been easy. When I was 25 years old, I gave birth to a son. We called him KK. The next thing that happened changed my life forever. He was struck by a card. That is the day I lost him. At only five years old, he was gone. His laughter, his love, his energy was all taken from me.

His laughter, his love, his energy was all taken from me.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：My life became a downward spiral
segments.original: My life became a downward spiral. I began to drink drinking lettuce, substance use. For the substance use, I was in prison. Every time I left prison, I swore I wouldn't go back, but I did. Over and over and over again. I remember one day standing in front of a judge and asking that judge, is there any help for me? And the judge sentenced me to prison one more time. No one cared. No one was listening. But when I walked into that room in 1997, I was ready to be heard. In the rooms of alcoholic synonymous, they listened. I took a deep breath and stood up and said, look what drugs and alcohol have done to me. The immediate compassion, empathy and love that rolled off these complete strangers was enough to put a sizeable dent in my pain, my shame, my guilt, and all that sorrow.

Every time I left prison, I swore I wouldn't go back, but I did. Over and over and over again. I remember one day standing in front of a judge and asking that judge, is there any help for me? In the rooms of alcoholic synonymous, they listened. I took a deep breath and stood up and said, look what drugs and alcohol have done to me. The immediate compassion, empathy and love that rolled off these complete strangers was enough to put a sizeable dent in my pain, my shame, my guilt, and all that sorrow.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：I kept talking and they kept listening
segments.original: I kept talking and they kept listening. I shared all the thoughts. I had spent decades trying to silence. As they listened, I began to heal. Listening saved my life and it opened the door. I got sober in Santa Monica and a fluent part of Los Angeles. And I noticed something there. People in Santa Monica, they weren't going to prison for substance use for alcoholism. And I thought, why didn't that judge give me a paper and say, Ms. Burton, A.A. was I not worth a piece of paper? Was I not worth direction toward a solution? So as I got stronger in my recovery, I thought about women just like me, cycling in and out of prison, looking for safety and not finding it. So I got a job, a minimum wage job. And I say $13,000.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：And I took $3,000 and I've been put d...
segments.original: And I took $3,000 and I've been put down on a house. And I bought some furniture. Every morning, I wake up and I go down to the Greyhound bus station where women leave in prison with dropped off. And I knew that station well because I had been dropped off there so many times for myself. And as they got off the bus carrying a trash bag of belongings and hoping their heart, I would walk up to them and I'd say, girl, I have a house. And if you want to come live there, it's a safe place to be. You can come live there. And before long, there was 11 of us living in that house. We cooked together. We went to meetings together. We shared resources. We laughed together. We cried together. But most of all, we healed together.

And if you want to come live there, it's a safe place to be. You can come live there. And before long, there was 11 of us living in that house. We cooked together. We went to meetings together. We shared resources. We laughed together. We cried together. But most of all, we healed together.

segments.title: 第 5 幕：Before long, people saw what I was do...
segments.original: Before long, people saw what I was doing and they joined me. And we created a team. Today, there's 12 houses across Los Angeles. Thank you. What we built was a house of women, helping women. Each house is staffed to support its residents who pay rent, do chores, buy groceries, and learn to be accountable responsible members of the community. We helped them find jobs, learn financial literacy, and help them with any legal issues. As the result, thousands of women have came back to the community and hundreds of mothers have been reunited with their children. In 2017, I published my memoir, Becoming Miss Burton, from prison to recovery to leading the fight for incarcerated women. In order to tell my story, I held book talks all over the nation, behind prison walls. There, I would listen to women.

segments.title: 第 6 幕：They were pleading for a place to go ...
segments.original: They were pleading for a place to go after they were released. They were sitting with tears streaming down their faces, wanting to rebuild their lives, to be reunited with their children, find a job in their community, break free from the criminal justice system. Every year in this country, around 2 million women are released from prisons and jails. They walk out with a trash bag of belongings, hoping someone will listen, hoping someone will help. When there's no help, when there's no safe place to land, too many of them will go back. I knew I could not provide resources of a new way of life to all those women. So I created safe, sisterhood alliance for freedom and equality, to replicate my model. Our first training was with 13 women. To date, we trained over 700.

segments.title: 第 7 幕：To listen, to create support, to give...
segments.original: To listen, to create support, to give hope. When women like me have safe housing, families reunify, recidivism drops, and community stabilize. I started with one house of women helping women. Today, there is a tire network of women helping women. In 20 U.S. states and also in Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria. We have replication down to a science. The leadership is there. The demand is there, and the goal is clear. More houses and more cities. More mothers reunite with their children. This is family preservation. This is community repair. When someone listened to me with compassion, regular than judgment, it changed my life. My story since that day in 1997 shows what is possible with people who have support, hope, and determination.

title: How AI is breaking the internet (and what to do about it)
chineseTitle: AI 正在摧毁开放互联网的基石（我们该如何拯救它）
speaker: Matthew Prince
speakerTitle: Cloudflare 联合创始人兼首席执行官
subCategory: 互联网生态与人工智能
quote: If the content creators who provide the raw knowledge for AI models can no longer get visitors or earn a living, the well of human knowledge will dry up for everyone.
quoteTranslation: 如果为 AI 模型提供原始知识的内容创作者不再能获得访客或维持生计，全人类的知识源泉都将为所有人枯竭。

spoken.meaning: 干涸、枯竭（比喻网络优质原创内容的消失）
spoken.quote: When users never leave the search page, the revenue for publishers begins to dry up completely.
spoken.pronunciation: /draɪ ʌp/ - dry 的 /aɪ/ 与 up 的 /ʌ/ 形成自然平滑连读。

spoken.meaning: 公平竞争的环境（强调小创作者与巨头平台之间的权利对等）
spoken.quote: We need to create a level playing field where independent publishers can monetize their content fairly.
spoken.pronunciation: /ə ˈlɛvl ˈpleɪɪŋ fiːld/ - level 与 playing 紧密相连，field 尾音 /d/ 饱满。

spoken.phrase: kill the goose that laid the golden egg
spoken.meaning: 杀鸡取卵（形容 AI 爬虫过度抓取内容却不给原作者回馈流量）
spoken.quote: By scraping everything without giving anything back, tech giants are killing the goose that laid the golden egg.
spoken.pronunciation: /kɪl ðə ɡuːs ðæt leɪd ðə ˈɡoʊldən ɛɡ/ - 经典习语，语调起伏分明，批判意味强烈。

grammar.name: Were it not for ... 虚拟语气倒装条件句
grammar.quote: Were it not for the open web, none of the LLMs we marvel at today could have existed.
grammar.explanation: If it were not for 的倒装省略形式，庄重有力地强调开放互联网不可替代的前提价值。

vocab.meaning: 直接回答引擎（区别于传统跳转网页的搜索引擎）
vocab.detail: 特指直接生成最终总结而不是提供外部网页链接的新一代 AI 搜索形态。

vocab.meaning: 抓取预算与版权补偿机制
vocab.detail: 指 AI 爬虫抓取网站数据时与出版商建立的流量或资金结算协议。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：The internet is an absolute miracle
segments.original: The internet is an absolute miracle. And for the last 30 years, it has been driven by very consistent and fundamental business model that has given us everything amazing about the internet and everything not so amazing as well. I run a company that provides a lot of the internet's infrastructure. And as a result, it means three things. One, we've had this unique view into what is going on online. Two, we care enormously about the success of the internet. And three, I think I can share with you some of how that underlying business model is changing and why it's important. Because as that business model changes, it's gonna have a dramatic effect on what the internet is, but beyond that, on what content is created, on what journalists get compensated for, on how researchers are able to do their research. And so it's up to all of us as that business model of the internet changes, to make sure it changes for something we want and can learn from the mistakes that we had in the past. So to review the past, let's look at what that business model was. And we all know it, basically, which was the internet was built on, we took an idea and we put it online, and then we drove traffic to that idea. And then from that traffic, we either sold things, subscriptions, or ads.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：And it's been pretty amazing to watch...
segments.original: And it's been pretty amazing to watch how that has very much driven the growth of the web and the growth of the internet over time. And it's survived a number of dramatic platform shifts. We all started browsing the internet on browsers, on our desktop or laptop, that transitioned to be increasingly social media, which was the interface through which we consumed content. And then we went to consuming it through our mobile devices. And yet, through all of this, the humble banner ad has basically financed it all. Traffic has been the currency of the internet, and that's what everyone has built their content to try to achieve. And if we want to look for who's the superman, who's the superhero that has driven this? For the last 27 years, that has been Google. Think about how much more of the way that you consume information already is looking at your AI chatbot and how much more of that will be the case in the future.

speakerTitle: Our World in Data 研究员 · 生物医学史学者
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Scientific breakthrough is only the opening act; translating discovery into affordable medicine is the real marathon.
quoteTranslation: 科学实验室的重大突破不过是序幕；将纯粹的科学发现转化为平价可及的救命良药，才是真正漫长险峻的马拉松。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：I've been writing about global health...
segments.original: I've been writing about global health and medical innovation for years. And when I tell my friends and family how much progress there's been, the reaction is almost always the same. They had no idea most of it was happening. Take the most common cause of death today, heart disease. People today have roughly a quarter the chance of dying from heart disease as people did in the 1950s at the same age. A quarter. Back then there were no status, no cholesterol testing, no implanted pacemakers, no anti-smoking campaigns, no bounds on trans fats, no bypass surgery, no CPR. But hardly anyone hears about the long-term impact of those breakthroughs. On progress happens gradually, it's rarely considered news. And I think it's a problem. I think it's part of why people don't know how important it's all been. Public health, vaccines, and all arrests, and improving people's lives. But what I want to tell you about is the thing that doesn't make the news at all. Not the breakthroughs themselves, but everything that got in the way of them. I used to have this impression that breakthroughs were uncommon, sporadic. Sometimes happening by pure chance, sometimes by sheer determination.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：The way I see it now, it's more like ...
segments.original: The way I see it now, it's more like there's a continuous stream of medical innovation every year. In just the last two years, for example, we've had a new anti-viral against HIV, which protects against infections with an efficacy of nearly 100%, which is the single dose given every six months. There are new drugs that reduce cholesterol levels by 60% beyond the effect of statins. There are new treatments that slow down the progression of certain cancers, certain lung cancers, brain cancer, and multiple myeloma by half or more. And in just the last five years, we've had new vaccines against four diseases for the very first time. COVID, of course, but also the first malaria vaccine, the first chicken guinea vaccine, and the first vaccine against RSV. The tools to develop new drugs and vaccines have improved enormously. Like genome sequencing, for example, which has touched almost every part of biology. Back when the human genome project was completed in 2003, it cost $50 million to sequence one person's genome. And it took half a year. Now, it takes under four hours. And it cost a few hundred dollars. There's also been a revolution in the technology of microscopes.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：Over the past 200 years, their resolu...
segments.original: Over the past 200 years, their resolution has increased over 10,000 fold. We can now see viruses down to their individual atoms and design new drugs to target them extremely precisely. Until the 1930s, no one had ever seen a virus. So, if our technology has advanced so much, why are so many diseases still untreatable today? What I've learned is that technology isn't always the barrier. Sometimes it's about the funding, the institutions and the incentives. We recently got a new malaria vaccine, as I mentioned, and when I first heard about it, I was amazed. I remember learning that malaria was a very complicated disease scientifically. It's caused by a parasite, not a virus or bacteria. And that parasite changed its shape multiple times during its life cycle, which makes it really hard to know what to target with a vaccine. So, I wanted to write about this amazing breakthrough. But one of the first things I learned about this new malaria vaccine that was introduced just a few years ago was that it was developed in the 90s, decades ago. The researchers who developed it struggled to find funding to test it at every stage of the process.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：There was no commercial incentive
segments.original: There was no commercial incentive. It's not profitable to develop new drugs and vaccines against diseases that affect people in poverty, in poorer countries. Even if millions of children might benefit, even if there's a huge economic benefit as well, it took foreign aid and philanthropy to fund the research to test it. And it literally took decades to reach the children who needed it. When I learned about this, I feel like there was nothing to celebrate. It seemed more like a failure. How could we let that happen? How could it take so long to test a vaccine that had already been developed? While half a million children were dying from malaria every year. Why wasn't that the story? Those children aren't coming back. But what I wanted to know was how we could prevent that from happening again. Like, what if we could change the economic incentives? Well, economists have come up with an idea to do just that. It's called an advanced market commitment. It's where donors commit to buying a vaccine at a certain price per dose. But only if it's developed and proven safe and effective. That commitment gives companies the confidence to invest in the first place.

segments.title: 第 5 幕：And it can bring vaccines into existe...
segments.original: And it can bring vaccines into existence that would otherwise never get made. And most importantly, it makes sure that they're manufactured at scale and sold in a affordable price. So they reached children who need them. That idea was used over a decade ago to help develop new vaccines against pneumococcal disease, which is a deadly bacterial infection of the longest. Vaccines already existed, but they didn't include the strains that were common in Africa and South Asia. So in 2009, several countries and philanthropists came together to fund an advanced market commitments for new vaccines. And it actually worked. People, companies developed them and they reached children much faster than usual. It's estimated that those vaccines have saved over 700,000 children's lives since then. This idea to fix market incentives is one way to speed up the process. But it's not the only thing we can do. Take childhood leukemia, for example. It used to be very difficult to test new treatments for the disease, because leukemia is rare. And individual hospitals struggle to find enough patients to run clinical trials. So researchers built networks across the US and later Europe and Canada to help recruit patients from all over those countries until larger clinical trials.

segments.title: 第 6 幕：That collaboration made it possible t...
segments.original: That collaboration made it possible to test treatments and learn what works faster. And it's why leukemia is no longer the disease it used to be. Before the 1970s, only around 15% of children with leukemia would survive even five years from a diagnosis. Now, that figure is 85%. Most children in richer countries today survive and are effectively cured of the disease. I want to give you another example. Back when I was at university, we had a substitute lecture one day on my course on infectious diseases. And she told us that our original lecture was away because he had gone to West Africa to do research to develop an Ebola vaccine. I remember sitting in that lecture theater at the back and I was thinking to myself, can you just do that? Can you just pack up and go? It hadn't even occurred to me and it made me realize that all of these breakthroughs came from people like him, people who changed their lives to make them happen. Or people who thought differently, whether they were scientists, economists, operators or managers, they created the incentives and institutions so that generations in the future, all of us wouldn't have to face the same problems that they did.

And it was hard to develop and test it for all the same reasons. There was a little commercial incentive and it was hard to run clinical trials because it was hard to predict where Ebola outbreaks would arise and vaccinate people in advance. So scientists came up with a different idea. They waited for individual cases of Ebola to appear and then quickly vaccinated all of the people around them, tested the vaccine that way. That idea called ring vaccination helps find a vaccine that we now know is very effective. Now these are just some of the ideas that people have had so far. But what I've learned from them is that breakthroughs don't just happen because we have the tools to make them. They depend on how innovation happens in the real world. And there's something else that I've learned from them that I've had much harder to stomach. Many of them might not have happened at all. So when I think back to that stream of innovation, all of those breakthroughs and all of that progress that we've seen, I do find it amazing.

segments.title: 第 8 幕：It's incredible
segments.original: It's incredible. But it also really frustrates me. That's how much progress we've made despite it being so hard. The good news is people have come up with ideas to change that. Some of them really work. Like the ones I've told you about today. And they just haven't been used enough. But we also need people to come up with new ideas and test them and scale them up to. It takes people who decide to persist despite that. And I think here it takes people who recognize something quite simple. That diseases are not a fact of life. They're problems that we can solve. Thank you.

title: Lessons: What to do when you get “layered” at work

segments.title: 第 1 幕：There's an experience that a lot of p...
segments.original: There's an experience that a lot of people go through at work. You start as an individual contributor. Then as your company grows, you get to hire and run a team. You're in the biggest job you've ever been in, and you're slightly overwhelmed all the time. Then one day, your manager sits you down and says, I think we need to bring in someone who has more experience to run this area. I want you to stay and work for them. That's called layering. When your manager decides to bring in a boss for you or split your job in half. It happens to a lot of people, but somehow we don't talk about it very much. And the thing about layering is that it sucks. Honestly, for everyone involved. And it can go really wrong and be really messy if it's not handled thoughtfully. Recently, you met my friend Don Foll. Don was most recently the CEO of CrossFit, formerly the CEO of Athos, a wearable startup. And before that, he was the head of operations at Pinterest. And before that, where I met him, he led all of operations for Facebook's users and developers. The thing is, early in Don's time at Facebook, he was layered. Cheryl Sandberg, the CEO at the time, decided to split his job in two. He did not take it well initially. Honestly, I was like, I, this isn't good. This is clearly a step back. I have clearly failed. I remember Cheryl Sand me at the time. Don, you will be better in, you will be better as by virtue of this. You will be better at your job. You will find that this gives you the ability to focus. And honestly, that's almost like that is all BS. That's what you say to the person who's job like, stop.

segments.original: So here's the thing. Even if layering is painful and unsettling, it is often a necessary and normal part of a company's growth. But learning how to navigate it well, that's really hard. And it's what this episode is all about. I'm Molly Graham, and this is Work Life, a show where we untangle the messy human side of work. Layering happens for a bunch of reasons. Because the business is growing so fast that it needs a leader who has seen this phase of growth before. Some people are strong individual contributors, but weak managers. And they should return to their previous roles for the sake of everyone's sanity. Sometimes the function has simply gotten too big for one person to run. In Don's case, he was running all of operations at Facebook for multiple departments, plus sales, plus the delicate work of risk and fraud. Cheryl would personally tell you that Don was the highest performing manager in the company. And his job was too big for him to do well, especially at a time when Facebook was scaling really quickly. Those three parts of the sentence don't seem to line up.

Even if you're layering someone, they're probably a respected part of your organization. And the way you treat them will send a message to everyone else about what they can expect when they take risks, when they need support. And most importantly, how you treat people, how they can expect to be treated as things change. So to recap, get clear on the problem. Make a concrete plan. Prepare for any reaction. And be honest every step of the way. That's it for this episode. Good luck out there. And reach out if you have any questions about this. Our email is worklife at TED.com.

segments.title: 第 1 幕：Making lifestyle changes to not only ...
segments.original: Making lifestyle changes to not only lose weight, but to maintain a healthy weight long term, is hard. Ask anyone who has ever tried. So let's consider my mom for instance. She is 77 years old and has struggled to maintain her weight in order to achieve good blood sugar control over the past 30 years. You see, good blood sugar control requires maintaining a delicate balance between diet, exercise, and insulin injections. So early in the COVID-19 pandemic last year, my mom came to stay with me, which led to a change in her usual dietary intake, away from meals provided to the elderly, to more helpful home cooked meals. What could possibly go wrong? Well, overnight her blood sugar drop dangerously low and she was incoherent and nearly unconscious. Imagine having to inject your mom with a giant horse needle of glucagon to boost her blood sugar until she could take in calories on her own. I was terrified that she would not be okay or that I might need to call for emergency medical treatment during the pandemic. Luckily, she responded to the emergency injection and was able to consume enough calories to bring her blood sugar back up. But of course, this led to a high blood sugar and she needed even more insulin, which is a fat storing hormone to get her blood sugar to a normal range. Although it took a coordinated effort with her doctor to find balance between her diet, exercise, and insulin regimen, I was happy to be social distancing with my mom. And she was able to lose some weight, even though she sometimes complained that I was acting like the food police. Nonetheless, I was grateful to have my biggest fan and run streak motivator with me during the lockdown. We became a village of two. Each day she would ask me, did you go run yet?

segments.title: 第 2 幕：You see, she would ride her stationar...
segments.original: You see, she would ride her stationary bike while I was working during the day and running at almost 10 p.m. It was a tough year to say the least, but at least this arrangement allowed us to create a healthy and supportive environment together. So the problem is we often think of weight control as an individual challenge. And of course, to some extent it is. But we know that the environments in which we live, learn, work, and play affect our ability to engage in helpful behaviors. When the world around us is what we might call an obese-identing environment, in other words, systemically and perpetually geared towards creating obesity, acting like weight loss or maintaining a healthy weight is a personal responsibility is simply not helpful nor effective. To put this in simple terms, I can't blame you for being overweight if restaurants and grocery stores or at least all the ones you can afford sell an abundance of high-sugar, high-calorie processed foods at low prices. And then if you don't have access to good health care and fitness options and work multiple jobs, you don't have time to exercise anyway. That's like time your hands behind your back pushing you into a pool and yelling that used to sweat. And if you have a genetic propensity towards excessive weight gain, long-term weight maintenance may simply be unattainable given the current treatments available. Although individual health behaviors are important for positive health outcomes, these behaviors are driven by the context in which we as individuals find ourselves. Imagine what we could do if we optimize systems, policies, and practices for our physical not to mention mental health. There are a lot of things that need to change, but that won't happen overnight, such as our work schedules, wages, the availability of healthy, affordable foods in every community and public spaces that make walking, biking, and hiking safe, accessible, and inviting. As a society, we need to start thinking about these things as not only luxuries, but essentials for a high quality, helpful life. But in the meantime, while we push collectively and national governments to take our health and the systems that facilitate health seriously, there are also things we can do right now on our own community by community.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：We know from research and animal and ...
segments.original: We know from research and animal and human populations that connections provided through social networks and communities are associated with better health and quality of life. So until we fix the systems that are harm in our health, we can all work to buffer the negative impact of these systems. Research also shows that individuals living in socially cohesive communities are at least those with strong social connections have better health outcomes than those who are more socially isolated. And these social environments work to combat obesity related behaviors and promote well-being, even in the face of systemic, obesity-genic conditions. And how do I know? My research team and I have been studying social environments and women's health. I've also observed the social support strategies of the women in my own network and their struggles with weight. Although their stories shed light on the lived experiences of navigating long-term health behavior change, how do they align with the science? In my work examining physical activity behaviors among black women, for whom the prevalence of obesity is disproportionately higher than white women in the United States, we have been able to describe aspects of the social context that support their success. Even among overweight, but active women, more than half engaged in physical activity with others for companionship, motivation, and accountability. One participant has stated that if my friends did not bug me, I would rarely work out. While another encouraged other women to get involved with a community that will push you towards your physical activity goals, she described the community as like-minded individuals. Also in our work with social physical activity the members said that friendship, motivation, encouragement, and accountability were the most important factors for supporting their long-term physical activity success. From conducting research on how social networks and social support strengthen our ability to achieve and sustain health goals and supporting a network of hundreds of women, I can tell you there are three things that all of us should consider. Number one, find or build yourself a tribe of like-minded individuals for motivation and accountability. This could be a tribe of two, like my mom and me or a group of individuals who enjoy walking in nature. Number two, create monthly wellness goals and share them with your tribe. One or two small changes and realistic expectations will do. And number three, celebrate your success. Don't just push each other but throw parties and uplift each other for making progress. Remember, maintaining a healthy weight takes more than diet and exercise.

segments.title: 第 1 幕：When I was in my early 30s, I was an ...
segments.original: When I was in my early 30s, I was an associate at a Wall Street law firm, and I had been working 16 hour days for seven years straight. And even though ever since I was four years old, I'd had this beautiful and impossible dream of becoming a writer, I was also pretty ambitious and on the verge of making partner. Or so I thought, because one day a senior partner named Steve Schalen knocked on my office door, Steve was tall and distinguished and very decent. And he sat down and he reached for the squishy stress ball on my desk. And he said that I wasn't going to be making partner after all. And I remember very badly wishing that I had a stress ball too, but Steve Schalen was using mine. And I remember feeling sorry that it had fallen to Steve to be the one to tell me this news, because he really was a good guy. And I remember bursting into tears right in front of him, such a non-partner-ish thing to do. But that very afternoon I up and left my law firm for good.

title: How citizens (not politicians) are building the future

They built an organization called Regen Melbourne to act as a catalyst for citizen activity.

segments.original: But at the same time, we're watching us policy makers take huge steps backward in clean energy transitioning. And then heavily subsidizing fossil fuels in order to make that artificially cheaper. How much does it matter that the US is backtracking on the climate transition? So it matters a lot. It's not enough to destroy this transition. At this point, the US is about 11% of global emissions. So a big deal, but not a decisive one. But America is also trying to prevent this transition in other countries. So for instance, when the president imposed tariffs on places, you could get out of your tariffs if you agreed to buy a lot of US liquefied natural gas. So Japan and the EU made promises along these lines to go do it. That role is kind of drug dealer to the planet is not a savory one. Truthfully, I think when we look back on this period, we will think that Trump's decision to go to war in Iran was one of the things that turned out to push the renewable revolution faster than almost anything else. Same more about that. Well, everybody in the course of a few weeks figured out that relying on a commodity that had to go through a 20 mile wide channel of water was not something you wanted. And America has been saying, well, import the energy from us instead. Trump keeps telling everybody. I don't think there's that many countries around the world who are eager to tie their future to Donald Trump's moods. So around the world, we've watched in the last six weeks as one statesman after another has said, you know, the president of Indonesia said we're going to build 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2028. The president of South Korea said, I can't sleep at night because I'm figuring out how we're going to get enough energy. We're committed to our own self sufficient clean energy going forward. Country after country are making it clear that this is the direction they're going to have to go in. So we could be witnessing as one of the externalities of war.

segments.original: This catalytic effect on solar. It's a kind of perfect storm because remember this has happened twice now in this decade. First was when Russia invaded Ukraine and gas supplies for especially Europe were cut off and now this. And they coincide. I mean, 15 years ago it wouldn't have mattered that much because there wasn't a affordable alternative. But now there's something better cleaner and cheaper. So it should be a no brainer for countries to figure out that this is where they need to go. Just in the same way that, you know, 15 years ago when the price of gas went up, what could you do? But now what you can do is go buy an EV and people are crowding into EV showrooms around the world. The only exception again is the US where we've made it very, very difficult to do that. Again, it's the US cutting its own throat. The auto industry is clearly going to be owned by the Chinese within a few years. Yeah, yeah, those $12,000. $12,000. Nifty cars. Right. Electric cars. Both EVs and solar, of course, require batteries. And then what you don't get into in your talk is this debate, right? Around the infrastructure. Around solar that is also resource dependent in its own way. What needs to happen to support solar at scale? Well, I mean, we should say there's no such thing as a free launch, but there are definitely more expensive lunches and less expensive lunches. And this is in the latter category. You have to go say get some lithium to build a battery. So you have to go mine it somewhere and we should do our best to mine it carefully and humanely. But once you mine it, then you put it in a battery where it sits doing its lithium thing when the battery degrades. Now we recycle it and get the lithium back out and start over again. When you go mine cool, what do you do with it? You burn it. You burn it. You burn it. The next day. And you have to go mine some more.

segments.original: They same them out the next day. I keep your system going. There's no recycling it. It just turns into carbon dioxide and heats up the planet. A fraction of what is mined. Exactly right. So we're moving to a less resource intensive paradigm. Okay. One of the things about all this is that because the technology keeps improving, there's a kind of wildly virtuous circle that emerges. So I put solar panels all over my roof 25 years ago back when they were pretty expensive. If you took down those solar panels now and there's no need to because they're still working fine. That's that's how much better we've gotten in that quarter century. So theoretically at a certain point not that far in the future, this should become a kind of closed loop system. segments.title: 第 12 幕：There, as I said, become wildly popul...
segments.original: There, as I said, become wildly popular across Europe. They're illegal everywhere in the US, except the state of Utah. And now we've launched big fight to get that same law passed everywhere else. We've got it in about 28 state legislatures. And last week both Virginia and Maine approved it. So by the end of the year, I think a good third of the country, you'll be able to go do this. Very cool. And on this topic of policy and regulation, where do you see the biggest roadblocks right now? Well, I mean, the biggest roadblocks obviously DC. They're doing horrible things. They're shutting down wind farms that are working. They're putting federal and off limits to solar panels. It's all just crazy obstruction in the service of the people who gave them large campaign donations. But since we can't affect that for the moment, we're fighting hard to elect new people so we can. But in the meantime, there's a lot that can be done at the state and local level. Americans pay three times what Europeans or Australians pay for rooftop solar. And it's not because the panels are more expensive. It's because we have way more regulation and bureaucracy. It takes months to put these things up. In the rest of the world, it's pretty much like buying a refrigerator. You just call somebody up. I want solar on the roof. You know, by Wednesday, they're up there hammering by Friday or connect it up. Instead of the months-long saga that it is here. And that's why 40% of homes in Australia, 35 or 40% have solar panels on the roof, which has in turn why Australia is producing so much solar energy that beginning in June, they're going to start handing it out electricity free every afternoon for three hours. That's a huge shift. And think of the Americans who would enjoy profit from having some free electricity. We've been talking about the need for systems change, investment at scale. What's the role of the individual in this transition? What can we be doing individually or at our family level, you know, if we're getting behind you in this fight?

segments.title: 第 13 幕：Well, so individuals of course can do...
segments.original: Well, so individuals of course can do things in their own home and they should in their own community. I'm proud that I've got solar panels on the roof and happy they connect to an EV. But let's be clear, we're not going to solve this thing one Tesla at a time. Sure. The most important thing an individual can do always is be less of an individual and join together with others in movements large enough to reshape public policy. So we started for instance third act a few years ago that organizes old people like me. Anyone over the age of 60 and we've got 120,000 Americans now engaged in this for the two things we organize around or protecting the climate and protecting democracy. And it turns out older people are fantastic at both these jobs. And so, you know, if you're of a certain age, tell your grandparents about a cinema or direction. There's lots of other groups that are doing the same kind of good organizing young people at the sunrise movement and things like that. Those are some great examples of coalition building. What gives you hope as we head into this really difficult 18 months? Are the weather is going to be as unpredictable as ever? Yeah, we're in for heavy weather the next year and the next probably the next century. But I do think that we can build with solar power in particular both energy systems that produce less carbon and are also somewhat more resilient in the face of disruption of all kinds. be it war or hurricane or whatever. And I think that in the process we bring things down to a slightly smaller scale that allows communities to strengthen. You know, I live in a small state in Vermont. Only 600,000 of us, but we spend two billion dollars a year importing fossil fuel into Vermont. We just right checked to Texas or Saudi Arabia or something every month. So, you know, thinking about what it would mean to have that two billion dollars close to home and thinking of the kind of community power that it builds.

segments.title: 第 14 幕：When people ask me, where should I mo...
segments.original: When people ask me, where should I move to be safe from global warming? Which they often do. The answer is there is no place that's safe from global warming. Every place faces its own perils. The place that you want to be is the place with good neighbors. Neighbors have been optional for the last hundred years in the Western world, but they're not going to be optional for the next hundred years. You need communities around you. And that's why I've been from what where I live. You know, I think it has a strong sense of community. But clearly there are lots of places like that. Think about the beauty we saw in Minneapolis this winter as people came together to defend their neighbors. You know, that's the kind of community you want to be in. Because the same community that can stand up to ice can stand up to heat as well. Well, Mcibin, thank you so much for sitting down with us and for all of your fantastic work. Thank you for the good conversation and what a pleasure to be a TED and just be surrounded by people who are deeply engaged in what we need to be engaged in. We're so glad you're part of the family. That was Bill Mcibin at TED 2026 and in conversation with me, at least you. The interview was recorded in April of 2027.

title: The infodemic — and the scientists fighting against it
chineseTitle: 信息瘟疫蔓延时代的科学保卫战：流行病学家如何击破伪科学谣言？
speaker: Jessica Malaty Rivera
speakerTitle: 传染病流行病学者 · COVID Tracking Project 传播主管
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Science is a process, not an immutable dogma; communicating nuance is our vaccine against hysteria.
quoteTranslation: 科学是一场持续探索的动态过程，而非一成不变的教条；清晰沟通其中的细微差别，才是我们抵御群体恐慌的最佳疫苗。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：Hi, Jessica
segments.original: Hi, Jessica. Hi. Could you tell us how you define the term leadership, especially as it relates to your work in public health and infectious disease epidemiology? Yeah. Leadership isn't always a word that is used necessarily in public health or epidemiology, but it probably has been much more in the last several years as we've just experienced with the pandemic. And one thing that I always saw that was needed and lacking in a huge gap in the training that I got was on making it make sense to people. And that was my opportunity to lead. That was my opportunity to say, how can we connect people to this work? It's very siloed. It's very separate. And if we're talking about things that influence people's decision making and risk budgets and relationships and how they build community, how can I step in and bridge the gap between academia, fancy institutions, and the public that it's intending to serve? And it seems like there really is no true or test of leadership that in moments where you're doing it in times of unfavourability. And we know right now that public health and science is being questioned, especially in the United States, but abroad. And so I'm interested to hear how you think about courageous leadership in times where your work, the very foundation of what you're doing, is unsupported. And in some cases, even under attack.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：Yeah
segments.original: Yeah. And potentially unpopular opinion is I do think science is political because we need good science to inform our politics. We need data to inform the policies that make decisions and make systems available to our public. And what the difference is though is that it shouldn't be politicized. And so what courageous leadership, what being bold in that space has looked like for me is saying that and connecting with lawmakers and connecting with advocacy groups and even doing a lot of that work myself to make that connection more clear. The more siloed we are when it comes to science and policy, the more opportunity there is for really dangerous mistruths and false claims and conspiracies to fill that gap. And so if we're not using the language of science and translating it to people who are making these laws and policies, understand them and the people who are using their votes and the voices to elect them, then we're missing an opportunity to really make sure that everybody is represented in these science policies. And I think to sort of take you back on what you're just saying here, you have stood at the center of sort of this tension of communicating these complex, unpopular truths in what can feel like a very emotionally charged environment. How do you practice care and encourage in leading in moments where it feels like the political and personal stakes are really high for people in your audience?

segments.title: 第 3 幕：Yeah, it's not easy
segments.original: Yeah, it's not easy. I think that when I look back in the last several years, the good outweighs the bad. But speaking truth, uncomfortable truth for some people has come at a great cost to myself, my safety, my family. I wouldn't go back and not do it. But I'd be remiss if I didn't include the fact that we're living in some pretty dangerous times where we're relitigating established truth. And a way that I have sought groundedness, a way that I have continued is to remind myself of that why, of the purpose that it is that my children who inspire me to do that work. And in finding solidarity with other scientists who are passionate about making science makes sense and informing people so that to me it's tools in a toolkit. I don't want to dumb anything down for anybody. I want to elevate people's literacy in science and complex things. I'm not expecting people to remember all the things that I have to remember about biology and immunology. That's asking too much. But I do think that these are important tools for people to have to navigate really dangerous information ecosystems right now. And I think there's a lesson there, not just how you can consume this information and think about it, but also as a leader. And I'd love to hear more about how you actually do this because of course you're doing this from the space of public health.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：But all of us are sort of navigating ...
segments.original: But all of us are sort of navigating what feels like a really divisive moment. And so how do you decide what is a great place for you to speak up for you? What is it better for you to be quiet? And is it good for you to take a stand? How do you make those decisions? Yeah. I got into public health because at the core of public health is altruism. It is a desire to reduce harm, to prevent disease, to increase people's opportunity for long life and thriving in that long life. And so my red line is when information, specifically harmful health information, challenges or jeopardizes those things. And I do think that when we're experiencing public health emergencies, we're kind of dealing with two outbreaks. We're dealing with an outbreak of pathogen and an outbreak of information. And information today is not neutral. And we need to recognize that that lack of neutrality means that that is probably an accelerating driver of that epidemic. And often is, and how do we address both? If sometimes get a little myopic with public health and just think about the one threat. And so I do think that having this big picture view of tandem outbreaks is the way we go forward with this. It's the way for me to say, I can't just think about all the interventions that we need to have.

title: How gratitude rewires your brain
chineseTitle: 感恩如何重塑大脑神经回路：一位脑瘤心理学家的自愈科学
speaker: Christina Costa
speakerTitle: 积极心理学研究员 · 脑神经科学教育者
subCategory: 神经科学与积极心理学
quote: Gratitude activates the brainstem to produce dopamine, signaling that we are safe and loved. Kiss your brain for all it endures.
quoteTranslation: 感恩会激活脑干释放多巴胺，向整个身体传递安全与被爱的信号。亲吻你的大脑，感谢它所承受的一切奇迹。

spoken.meaning: 亲吻你的大脑（作者自创并风靡的感恩身体、赞美心智的仪式化动作）
spoken.quote: I would often ask my students to kiss their brain as a practice of gratitude for the work they did.
spoken.pronunciation: /kɪs jɔːr breɪn/ - 语气轻快温暖，kiss 与 your 自然连缀。

spoken.meaning: 困境中的一线光明、乌云背后的金边
spoken.quote: Gratitude isn't about ignoring pain; it's about looking for the silver lining without denying reality.
spoken.pronunciation: /ə ˈsɪlvər ˈlaɪnɪŋ/ - silver 前重后轻，lining 发音舒缓柔和。

spoken.meaning: 重塑大脑神经通路（神经科学核心术语，常用于日常心理赋能）
spoken.quote: Consistent gratitude practices literally rewire our neural pathways toward optimism.
spoken.pronunciation: /ˌriːˈwaɪər ˈnjʊərəl ˈpæθweɪz/ - rewire 与 neural 音节清晰分明。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：day
segments.original: day. When I was a middle school science teacher, I would often ask my students to kiss their brain. I got this idea from visiting my friend's kindergarten classroom. She would ask her students to kiss their brain and they would take their fingers, tap them to their mouth, and then to the top of their head, and it truly was as cute as you can picture it to be. So I decided to bring it back to my middle school classroom, which could have gone one of two ways, but it ended up being a really fun ritual for us too. And I would ask them to kiss their brain for all the work they did in class as a practice of gratitude. After teaching middle school, I came back to grad school to get my PhD in psychology. My research is within the area of positive psychology, which is a science that investigates the strengths and factors that allow individuals and communities to thrive. I also get to teach psychology to undergrad students and high school students. I love teaching psych, and my absolute favorite unit to teach in intro psych is the brain. But while I love teaching about the brain, I thought it would be pushing it to ask my undergrads, aka adults, to kiss their brain. So three years would go by before I would remember that fun phrase. One day after teaching, last year, I had a terrible migraine that left half of my face numb and blurred my vision. The migraines kept happening, I saw multiple doctors, and then I started experiencing dizzy spells. The neurologist ordered an MRI, and I remember being so excited because then I would be able to use my own brain pictures when I taught brain imaging to my students. But as it turns out, my MRI wasn't too picture perfect. The doctor called me and asked me to go to the ER because there was a large mass in the right hemisphere of my brain. I have never been more scared in my life than I was that night, and with tears dripping down my face in the hospital, I kissed my brain for the first time since I had left my middle school classroom. I made it my mantra, and I kissed my brain every single day leading up to and after surgery. Then, two weeks later, after surgery, the pathology reports came back, and I was diagnosed with an anoplastic astrocytoma. The weeks following were very difficult. segments.title: 第 2 幕：I hated the suggestion of naming my t...
segments.original: I hated the suggestion of naming my tumor something awful because the reality is that it was going to be my neighbor for the rest of my life, and I hated the guided imagery training that asked me to picture chemo as an army coming to battle the cancer cells because I didn't want to spend over a year of my life at war with my own body. I can see how these elements of the fight narrative can be empowering for people, but for me, I knew it wasn't going to work. So I started to reference well-being practices that I had learned from my own studies. Doctors always laugh with me when they find out that I'm a bio-psych and neuroscience major and it's like PhD student. Then when they ask what I'm studying and I tell them I study resilience and well-being, they either laugh again, say something like, oh, that's irrelevant or go, ah, the irony was never lost on me. I have read so many stories and studies of resilience, but I never pictured the day that I would have to personally experience it. I read and taught about gratitude practices specifically as a well-being strategy, and even though I knew the positive effects, I had never seriously practiced them myself. I started to incorporate some of these exercises into my life. I tried to stop focusing on what my body had done wrong and focus on the gratitude I had for my body instead. And really I realized this was something I had been doing when I was kissing my brains those days leading up to and after surgery. Gratitude became the tool that helped me restructure my vision of illness and disability when the world was telling me I should fight it instead. Instead of thinking about if I would be able to have kids one day, I thought of how amazing it was that my brain, despite its trauma, was able to deliver the perfect amount of hormones to my body to produce enough eggs to save for a later date. Every time I went to radiation and was put in my mask, I kissed my brain and I focused on the resident telling me how the healthy cells would be able to repair over time and the cancer cells could not. And when the operative notes came back for my surgery, a day that I remember very well and had been scared to think about, I read the note out loud, sobbing, happy and grateful tears, thinking about what my neurosurgeons team did. I started to feel such an immense sense of gratitude for science, medicine and my medical team that those thoughts started to drown out the what is my life going to be like thoughts. The more I practiced gratitude, the more peace I felt my situation and this got me interested in what could be happening with the science of gratitude at a neurological level. There are several positive psychological and social outcomes of gratitude, like increases in happiness, decreases in depression, having stronger relationships and experiencing positive emotion. And FMRI studies show us that several parts of our brain and pathways are activated when we experience and express gratitude. One of these parts is the medial prefrontal cortex, an area associated with the management of negative emotions. Together, these changes in neurotransmitters and hormones combined with the activated neural pathways help us cognitively restructure potentially harmful thoughts to better manage our circumstances.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：And the cool thing is that we can int...
segments.original: And the cool thing is that we can intentionally activate these gratitude circuits in our brain. In general, the more we do something the easier it becomes and our brains work the same way. The more we activate these gratitude circuits, the less effort it takes to stimulate those pathways the next time and the stronger those pathways become. Neuroplasticity is a term I teach my students that refers to our brains ability to form new neural connections throughout life, which means this is something that anyone can practice and get better at over time. So I kept practicing gratitude even when it seemed impossible. I continued to thank my brain for the amazing work it does as I prepare for 12 more rounds of chemo this year. I write down three things I'm grateful for and why I'm grateful for them no matter what every morning that I wake up. I write thank you notes to my heroes in healthcare, nurses who get the IVN the first time, the anesthesiology resident who held my hand during the awake portions of my surgery, radiation therapists that play my playlist during treatment and administrative staff that makes me smile every time I walk into the hospital. I do want to take a second here and practice what I teach to shout out my doctors and their teams from the Michigan Medicine multidisciplinary brain tumor clinic. I have never met such intelligent, kind, and patient people. Thank you for making me feel brave when I sometimes felt the opposite. I think the universe might think it's funny that a psych instructor and researcher who studies well-being ended up with a brain tumor. The truth is that we need more awareness and more research regarding brain tumors and brain cancer. Doctors can't exactly predict how my tumor will behave and really none of us can predict what our lives are going to be like exactly. But what I hope I can show you is that we can also be grateful for the unexpected challenges. I don't want to dismiss people who may find the fight narrative empowering. I also don't want to suggest that it's by any means easy to find ways to be grateful in dealing with adversity. This has been the hardest thing that I've ever had to do. But I do want to empower those that feel like me, that there's another way to go through whatever your journey may be, that loving your body doesn't have to be conditional, and that by practicing gratitude we can actually wire our brains to help us build resilience. And lastly, I hope everyone, no matter where you are or what you are doing, can take a second to kiss your own brain and thank it for all that it does for you.

title: How I turn joy into art

rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Color is not superficial decoration; color is a powerful language of hope, memory, and inclusion.

segments.title: 第 1 幕：My name is Yinca Elori, an artist, de...
segments.original: My name is Yinca Elori, an artist, designer, a storyteller, a dreamer, and a person who lost color. I believe that as my calling and mission is to bring joy to the world. We live in a time when we everyone is asking the same question. Who am I and what brings me joy? Looking back now, I realize this question has followed me my whole life. My job was always present in my life and always around me. I just didn't have the language for it. But what I did have was a world which of color, symbols, dreams, and affirmation. I grew up in London in 27 Ashby House on the Councillor state. I was raised by my dear parents who moved to London in the 1980s. My mother from Ondo State coined the Sunshine State. It's known for its majestic rock landscapes and warm weather. The people there are warm, grounded, and strong. My father from Iqiti State in southwest Nigeria are placed known for its nature and famous for its warm and cold springs.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：A place called incongousy, and known ...
segments.original: A place called incongousy, and known as the founder of knowledge. Because of its reputation for academic excellence and intellectual achievement. Even before I had been to these places, I could picture myself growing up there, being raised there. But I was born and raised in London. I felt a strong sense of connection and a strong sense of belonging. So a place I called home. In the UK, my beloved mother did many things. She bought and sold Swiss filets. She catered for weddings and birthdays. She was an architect of joy, architect of bringing people and things together. In our glass cabinet at home, she would collect objects of memories she treasured and I showed glass. My dad worked in retail. Everyone called him Uncle Pool. He was everyone's uncle, dad, brother, mentor, and therapist. He brought so much joy to the workplace. I won't point my parents also owned a corner shop in London. It was insane that all the kids after school, people in the estate, the neighbors, passersby, would come to the corner shop.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：This place became a gathering point f...
segments.original: This place became a gathering point for the whole community. On Sundays, my mom and dad would host church services. They would leave lectures and sermons. The words of worship and affirmation, singing and moving have manifested in my memory. My parents loved house parties, live music, placed of jewel of fries for weaving in our small towns of float, different languages, different journeys, all in one room. My parents brought all these rituals of community and faith and pleasure with them from Nigeria to the UK. As a child, I didn't realise I was experiencing a daily baptism of joy. I'd enjoyed that being passed on from generations of generations, without even knowing it. Every ritual, every gathering, every exchange, carried a deep, simple meaning. All these were seeds of joy. How did I have this joy? Myself, I developed my mother the same collective spirit. She collected objects, I'd like symbols, a sun, a rock, hands, a star, a talking drum. At first, I didn't know why I was drawn to these symbols, but I realised these symbols were memories of things I enjoyed and things that brought me joy as a youth.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：The undoes sunlight, the rituals, the...
segments.original: The undoes sunlight, the rituals, the community, the gatherings. The visualising them helps me harvest joy. Visual storytelling is how my story is really carry. This is what I do in my work. I don't invent stories. I uncover them. I really imagine them through my lens. Similar to how I reflect on my personal experiences, I listen to people's stories and experiences and turn them into symbolic symbols. Because when you visualise something, when you share it, you can pass it onto someone else. Another generation. This is why I think joy is transgenerational. We can inherit it from what it was before, or what surrounds us. This is what I did in the recent experiment that asked my friends for my audience. What does joy look like for you today? What is your early memories of joy looking like for you today? And I could be translated into symbols that connect with your memories. Receiving and abundance of responses felt like I was receiving another daily baptism of joy, just like my parents' rituals.

segments.title: 第 5 幕：I selected some of the answers and tu...
segments.original: I selected some of the answers and turned them into symbols. A mushroom, a cashew tree, a sports car, a palm wine cup. And I paired them up with symbols from my archive, riffles of laughter, precious joy, connection, sunrise, and community. This selection was based on what happened the most. Around 80% of the responses carried a sense of togetherness. Through connection shared inherited, not individual. Around 5% of the responses were connected to nature, plants, sunlight, open space, feeling through light, texture, and smell. About half of the responses spoke about freedom, movement, exploration, anticipation, nervous fictions. Some were talking about growth and always been immediate, sometimes it was at a time, sometimes we struggle. A small number spoke about stillness. So I took all of these impressions and turned them into an artwork, an artwork that celebrates the power of trans-generational joy when it comes together, this to magic you can create. But what stood out to me the most was that no one spoke about personal achievement.

segments.title: 第 6 幕：It was always about people and places...
segments.original: It was always about people and places and shared experiences. All of my responses were very visual already. It's something we often recognize in hindsight. To me, harvesting trans-generational joy means finding the seeds that were planted before you, by your parents, by your loved ones, by your community. My parents always said to me, whatever you sow is what you shall reap. I hope today you all reap joy, pass it on from person to person, and generation to generation. It was passed on to me and now I want to pass it on to you. Thank you.

vocab.meaning: 心理防御机制 / 戒备心理
vocab.detail: 个体遭遇外界评价或威胁时自发启动的抵触、否认或转嫁责任的本能保护反应。
指能够清晰指导下一步具体行为改进、并持续监测成效的高质量沟通体系。

segments.original: One of the most important lessons that I had to learn in my life is that when it comes to our growth and development there is no substitute for a tough piece of feedback from someone who cares about us and When we can make it safe enough for the people in our lives to tell us those hard things It not only benefits us. It can spark transformation in our workplaces and in our families and I learned this lesson the way that I learned most things which is the hard way and And it was when I got a tough piece of feedback from my best friend at work Christy so I met Christy years ago when I left the only organization I had ever worked for to start over at a new company and I was freaking out and Christy was this incredibly kind and welcoming person who just really went out of her way to help me be successful and we became fast friends and And then one day we got into an argument Not uncommon for us. We're both pretty stubborn and opinionated people and we resolved it and I Thought everything was fine She had a very different reaction and the next day she came in and she gave me this feedback and I'll never forget it she said It just seemed like while we were arguing That you needed me to feel stupid and if you've ever had somebody make you feel that way, you know, it's it's awful So here's my best friend at work Somebody that I care about she's told me that I've heard her and so of course my immediate reaction is I get very defensive. So I remember running through all of this in my head, right? Like How could you say that that's completely unfair?

segments.original: But where this really broke open for me was one day when I was talking to my sister and I was I was telling her the story and how hey somebody at work said I can come across as arrogant and condescending Can you believe that? and she paused and She said yeah, and I was completely blindsided Which doesn't make any sense of course because she would have been one of the first people to have to deal with this And it turns out I'd have bothered her for a long time But she hadn't talked to me about it And she told me there were times in my life that I really needed you But I didn't call because I just didn't want to hear that tone and that was so painful to hear And it was the breakthrough moment in our relationship Because now when she has a problem with me she could just tell me and that has meant everything to us and After that I was like I got to get feedback from everyone So I do this with with my boss with my teammates. I do this with my wife and son My son will say to me dad. Can I give you some feedback? I love it. I love it Usually yeah, I like I don't always agree with it But I'm such a better dad because of it and more important than that is it means everything to me that he feels safe enough to say that to me And I've also had the opportunity to help hundreds of other people create similar experiences in their own relationships Most of us we want to have these important and difficult conversations But we put too much pressure on the Christie's of the world to show up again and again with the courage to say the hard thing and that's a mistake There's too many barriers to that happening consistently as feedback receivers We have to make it safer and we have to lower the amount of courage that it requires to have that conversation Now thankfully this is a skill that we can learn and that we can practice And if you want to you can use an approach that I use called receiving feedback with tact So if you want to try this pick someone in your life that you want some more feedback from someone who cares about you But they'll be honest with you if you make it a little bit safer Then don't wait for them to give you feedback go out and ask for it Just don't make the mistake that I made early on I was working with this group of managers and I said go out and get some feedback from some of your employees and they're like, okay How am I doing as your manager and everyone was like great?
