segments.title: 第 5 幕：Why It's too scary, right? We need to...
segments.original: Why It's too scary, right? We need to we need to narrow that question. So I might say I want to get better at running our staff meetings What's one piece of advice you have for me and how I could improve? And then here's the key. It's how you respond That's going to be the difference between you learning something and building trust with this person or the opposite So when they give you the feedback that you asked for you can respond with tact so that stands for thankfulness Acknowledgement commitment and then we'll end where we began a second. Thankfulness. So that first thankfulness You're trying to calm down that like initial fight or fight response that you might both be experiencing So I might say that wasn't easy to hear but I'm really glad you're willing to say it With acknowledgement you want to make the other person feel seen and heard first because that's your entryway into an authentic Dialogue they're expecting you to defend yourself and all that's going to do is it's just going to shut them down or gear them up for a fight You don't have to agree Just acknowledge what they said acknowledge the feelings underneath what they said and then you can have a real conversation And that'll eventually lead you to some kind of a commitment if you agree with the feedback It could be the behavior change you're going to make if you don't agree or you're not sure It could be to gather a few more perspectives and circle back It could be that you need a little bit of time and space to process But you're going to get back to them at a specific date and time just be clear what's next and follow through and The second thankfulness is my favorite part because it's so easy to do and it's very powerful What you're trying to do here is reinforce and reward the behavior so that they keep doing it Like most of us don't do things that are you know painful or unpleasant like giving feedback Unless there's some sort of a benefit for doing it. So when the conversations over send them a quick text Thank you, right or do what one of my colleagues did when I gave him tough feedback He wrote me a handwritten. Thank you card Just do something that makes it feel like it was worth the risk to tell you So it's thankfulness acknowledgement commitment and then a second thankfulness Do this consistently and you're going to be amazed at what you learn and the ways that it starts to benefit your relationships There is likely someone in your life who cares about you and has something to tell you that you might not want to hear But it could change your life if you did if you want the benefits of that feedback ask for it and then respond with tech I have seen it do wonders for so many people including me as I was preparing for today. I shared a draft with my sister and this is what she told me. She said Chris you've completely flipped the way that you talked to me and I can't even remember what you used to sound like I Can be completely myself around you even though we're so different So go out and get a tough piece of feedback from someone who cares about you and let it change your life. Thank you That was Chris Wheatley

title: Idiots are everywhere. Here's how to cope
chineseTitle: 身边到处充斥着自以为是的人：我们究竟该如何体面相处与自保？
speaker: Joshua Johnson
speakerTitle: 资深公共广播主持人 · 艾美奖获奖记者
rawAdTrimmed: 已剔除片头片尾赞助广告
quote: Dismissing people as fools is lazy; understanding their underlying fear is where real power begins.
quoteTranslation: 轻率地将意见相左者斥为蠢蛋是智力的懒惰；唯有洞悉他们咆哮背后深藏的恐惧，真正的掌控力才悄然诞生。

segments.title: 第 1 幕：Idiots are everywhere
segments.original: Idiots are everywhere. Some people drive you right up the wall with their opinions, their attitudes, their politics. I don't with all kinds of people in my 20 plus years as a broadcast journalist. Eventually I found moderating tough conversations with whatever kind of difficult people you just thought of. Kind of simple to do, not easy, but simple. The trick is to go somewhere I know you'd rather not be. Closer. Distance makes things worse. I came up in public radio trained by old school journalists who taught me the art of neutrality. You neutralize your opinions, dead in your emotions and you can get through most conversations without rolling your eyes. Generally it worked and it built me a strong reputation for fairness, but when the subject matter felt personal, neutrality felt phony. I used to host a national talk show on NPR called One-A and in one of our early programs I interviewed a descendant of Confederate soldiers.

Generally it worked and it built me a strong reputation for fairness, but when the subject matter felt personal, neutrality felt phony. I used to host a national talk show on NPR called One-A and in one of our early programs I interviewed a descendant of Confederate soldiers.

segments.title: 第 2 幕：He argued that Confederate monuments ...
segments.original: He argued that Confederate monuments should be historically preserved. Now as a black man I felt enormous pressure to remain neutral so I decided I was just going to focus on his arguments instead of on him. His logic felt kind of flimsy and I called him on it and eventually he just folded and he said it really doesn't matter what I said. In the moment he said that I knew I had failed. I may have had a point but I missed a huge opportunity to really do my job. See my neutrality allowed me to interrogate his beliefs but the distance prevented me from seeing why he believed them. What if I had asked better questions like who influenced you the most informing these views? Suppose we let all of these monuments and statues stand just as they are. What would that mean to you? Getting his story might have shown me him behind his canned arguments grilling him changed nothing.

segments.title: 第 3 幕：It felt pointless
segments.original: It felt pointless. When you consider someone problematic there's a better way to deal with them, keep your sanity and maybe even connect and it sounds insane. Move closer. Not to embrace them but to explore them like a doctor studying a sample. You need a microscope, not a telescope. Doctors actually helped me learn this way before I became a journalist. As a teenager I was part of a summer program for future doctors. Clearly it worked. I found myself working with clinicians studying cancer and thrombosis and HIV, very serious conditions. I kind of naively expected them to be these crusading scientists but they were just level-headed people doing their jobs. But there was a lesson in that level-headedness. See I am not neutral about the cancers in our world. Biggatory hoaxes, political violence. I want them gone. However, as a journalist I often had to deal with them in my clinic on the air. I survived it by getting as close to those problems as I could and studying them like samples in a petri dish.

segments.title: 第 4 幕：In other words, I had to shift from n...
segments.original: In other words, I had to shift from neutrality to objectivity and know they are not the same. Objectivity is just when you park your emotions and learn without judgment. I don't have to like it. I am just here to learn from it. Neutrality negates your opinions. As if you have no judgments. Does anyone here honestly believe I have no opinions on race? Right. Now, notice I said park your opinions. When you park your car, you don't abandon it in the garage. You're coming back for it. So you can choose when to focus inward on what you think or outward on what you can learn. Of course sometimes your car ain't where you left it and maybe your opinions will move to. That maybe is why objectivity feels so vulnerable. That's why it works. That vulnerability is a sign of openness and a conversation that's not open is pointless. But if you can stay open, amazing things can happen.

segments.title: 第 5 幕：Another time on NPR was interviewing ...
segments.original: Another time on NPR was interviewing a former Baltimore police officer who would become this fiery advocate for law enforcement reform and he was going on and on just the long rant in autopilot just knowing and knowing and knowing and knowing and knowing and knowing. And I was trying to stay objective and listening is best I could. And I thought I heard his voice waver just a little. And in that waver I detected more than his rage. It sounded like trauma. So near the end of the interview I mentioned hesitantly that he seemed traumatized by his experiences as a top and could he reflect on that. He said I put people in prison cells who are better people than me. Whoa. Sure enough he went right back to his talking points but it didn't matter because in that moment that sliver of his story his defenses dropped and he shifted from being right to being real. Look, some people are just difficult but we can deal with them more simply.

segments.title: 第 6 幕：Here are three tips to get you started
segments.original: Here are three tips to get you started. First, get the story particularly the key decisions and the turning points. What someone believes is not as important as how they chose to believe it. Second, my NPR host pro tip, keep your questions short. Ten seconds tops. Long questions can feel like a setup or like your ramblings. And third, use that mental microscope. Look as closely as you can remember you don't have to like it but learn from it. It is time to reconnect even to the people you can't stand but this time we're going to make those connections count. You could learn a lot from an idiot especially if you resolve never to act like one. I really appreciate you all making time for me today.

Long questions can feel like a setup or like your ramblings. And third, use that mental microscope. Look as closely as you can remember you don't have to like it but learn from it. It is time to reconnect even to the people you can't stand but this time we're going to make those connections count. You could learn a lot from an idiot especially if you resolve never to act like one. I really appreciate you all making time for me today.

segments.title: 第 1 幕：Hi everyone, I'm Helen Walters
segments.original: Hi everyone, I'm Helen Walters. I am Head of Media and Curation at Ted. Welcome to another edition of Ted explains the world with political scientist Ian Bremer. Today we are going to explain the current and future states of the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Ian, as always, thank you so much for being here to help us try to make sense of things. Hi Helen, good to be back with you. Alright, let's start in Iran, which is now entering its sixth month of conflict with the United States. And in just the last two weeks we've seen attacks, we've seen counter attacks. None of the major issues between the two nations seem to be coming anywhere close to being resolved. So what is your read of what is going on and what should we actually be paying attention to? So I guess there are two different components that we need to think about. The first is why it is that the war is still going on given the clear costs to everyone involved. in the United States around the world and to the Iranians. And the second is how might we think about the potential for resolution. So first why is it happening? Because we had a memorandum of understanding that was signed between the US and the Iranians. And it was only a matter of weeks before that fell apart. The issue here is that President Trump and the Iranian military leadership really fundamentally disagree about how much leverage they each have over the outcome. This is very different from what we saw between Trump and Xi Jinping. When he hit out really hard on the tariffs and created a functional boycott and the Chinese hit back with their own tariffs. And then the critical minerals licensing regime and Trump realized I do not want to get into a tit for tat continued fight with the Chinese. This is going to hurt me too much. I need to back away and I need to ensure stability. The Iranians have hit Trump back pretty hard hit the Americans back. They've hit them back in blocking the straight and they've hit them back in attacking targets across the Gulf. Both infrastructure targets and American bases. But the Iranians believe they can continue to do that until they have control over the straight until they're given that control by the United States. Seated to buy the United States so that they are able to get a lot of money and determine who doesn't go through. President Trump's perspective is yeah, they may have been able to disrupt the straight. But I can continue to blow these guys up and ultimately they're going to have to capitulate.
